D. The supervisor will coordinate with the assigned King County Search and Rescue Coordinator or other resources, as required.

sections.title: V.I.P. Security
paras: Principle: In the event a Very Important Person (VIP) or dignitary visits or stays within the City of Federal Way, the Federal Way Police Department may participate in security upon request.
Practice: When assistance is requested, the Police Department shall prepare a plan to include, at the minimum, the following provisions.
A. A specific individual designated to prepare the plan and coordinate the department’s involvement.
1. If actual security is required, the SWAT Commander should be considered for this assignment.
B. The Police Department resources required for the requested security.
1. The need to deploy specialized units.
C. Coordination of communications with Valley Communications and other outside agencies.
After-Action Report: An after-action report shall be completed by the designated individual evaluating the provision of police services during the event.

sections.title: Special Events
paras: Principle: The Federal Way Police Department strives to ensure public safety by providing adequate and appropriate police services for special events. Special events include parades, street fairs, public demonstrations, labor strike activity, athletic events, and other activity that impacts traffic and crowd control. Refer to Standard 46.2.6 for specific practice related to dignitary and VIP security.

Practice: The various events will require special planning specific for that event. Therefore each special event shall have a Special Order prepared for the event by a designated commander. The Special Order shall include the following information at a minimum.
A. The person designated to act as the supervisor and/or coordinator for the provision of police services during the event.
B. The required traffic control and crowd control for the event. The resources required to provide adequate police services in this area.
1. An estimate of expected crime problems and a contingency plan to address crime problems.
2. An estimate of expected civil disturbances and a contingency plan addressing the considerations provided in Standard 46.1.10.
C. Use of special operations personnel when appropriate.
D. Coordination for outside agency involvement.
After-Action Report: The designated individual shall complete an after-action report evaluating the provision of police services during the event.

sections.title: Event Deconfliction: Event deconfliction is the process of determining when law enforcement personnel are
paras: Event Deconfliction: Event deconfliction is the process of determining when law enforcement personnel are conducting events in close proximity to one another or investigating the same people or the same problem at the same time. By notifying a central location of a planned event prior to its execution, officers will not unknowingly target or conflict with another law enforcement officer or compromise another investigation. It becomes especially critical when operating in concurrent or contiguous jurisdictions that are involved in high risk activities such as undercover operations, surveillance, fugitive apprehension, etc. Event deconfliction, along with the sharing of event and investigative information with other law enforcement agencies, and proper case activation procedures enhance officer safety and the efficiency of criminal investigations.

A. Deconfliction Process: As an agency we engage in event deconfliction in an attempt to avoid dangerous confrontations and/or unintentional consequences for law enforcement personnel and our citizens by entering qualifying events into the RISSafe system (or, if technology or programs change, any other system which has been approved for use department-wide by the Chief of Police or his/her designee). All information entered into this system is considered confidential and law enforcement sensitive.
The following steps and/or considerations will apply to the use of a deconfliction system.
1. Qualifying Events: Any activity or event that is pre-planned and also requires an operations plan (see MOS 43.1.5) shall be entered into the event deconfliction system. This includes:
• surveillance;
• raid operations;
• decoy operations;
• undercover operations;
• or any other high risk or special investigation that would benefit from event deconfliction.

2. Entry of Information: Personnel conducting field operations as described above shall ensure that these operations are entered into the event deconfliction system either online or by telephone at 800-952-5258. The individual assigned responsibility for writing/developing the operations plan will also be responsible for ensuring all necessary information has been entered into the event deconfliction system. All operations requiring entry into the event deconfliction system shall be made as soon as information is available, but at least two hours prior to the event taking place, if possible.
Information entered into the deconfliction system shall include:
1. Date and time of planned operation;
2. Type of operation;
3. Location of the operation, including any staging areas;
4. Information about the suspect(s), including full names, aliases or monikers, date of birth, vehicle information, phone numbers, contraband to be purchased and amount of money involved;
5. Lead and participating agency names;
6. Name and agency of the person entering the operation, including cellular telephone number, along with a secondary point of contact for the operation.
7. Specify the radius of deconfliction (if not preset by the deconfliction system).

3. Conflict Resolution: If a conflict with other law enforcement activity is identified both of the contact personnel will be notified by the event deconfliction system or watch center personnel. Each affected law enforcement entity is responsible for contacting one another and resolving the conflict before taking further action. Investigating personnel must refrain from executing any operations until identified conflicts have been resolved. Unresolved operational conflicts will be immediately referred to command/supervisory level personnel. Any exemption or deviation from this procedure shall be considered on a case-by-case basis and approved only by a command/supervisory level officer.

4. Training and Access: All personnel with assignments that may require them to perform event deconfliction shall receive training enabling them to obtain appropriate security access and to navigate through the event deconfliction system. Training is available through the Western States Information Network (WSIN).

B. Target and Investigative Information Deconfliction: Event deconfliction applies to geographical conflicts that occur at the same time and in the same proximity. Target and investigative activity deconfliction applies to subjects, gangs, locations, telephone numbers, vehicles, and other investigative information about criminal activity.

1. Upon opening an investigation of any crime primarily related to drugs, prostitution, or gangs, or a crime that extends beyond the jurisdictional boundaries of the city of Federal Way, information should be queried and/or stored through available and appropriate resources (e.g., WSIN) to determine whether another agency has an ongoing investigation with common investigative information, to reduce parallel investigations and to promote investigative collaboration. If a conflict is discovered in either target or investigative activity, contact shall be made with the other agency to resolve and coordinate issues and information.

sections.title: Tactical Operations: Outside Our Jurisdiction
paras: Principle: The law enforcement agency with primary territorial jurisdiction needs to be notified of all preplanned tactical operations that occur at addresses within their jurisdiction. All agencies should continue to require their officers/units to make courtesy notifications to the agency with primary jurisdiction whenever they are conducting other law enforcement type activities (i.e., surveillance, buy-bust operations and arrests) at locations outside of their own agency’s territorial jurisdiction.
Definitions:
A. Command Level Officer (internal): An individual with the official rank and title of Commander (or of Acting Commander), the Deputy Chief, and Chief of Police.

B. Command Level Officer (external): In terms of whom we should contact at another jurisdiction, it will be either a person with the official rank and title of Commander or, in agencies with a rank structure that includes Sergeant, our contact will then be at the Lieutenant rank or higher.
C. Agency with Primary Jurisdiction; The agency with the responsibility to provide routine police services at a given address is the agency having primary jurisdiction.

D. Preplanned Tactical Operation: Any situation not including fresh pursuit in which Federal Way police officers or detectives deploy with the intent to arrest an offender or serve a search warrant at a known location. This does not include typical or mainstream crimes being investigated by Federal Way officers/detectives occurring exclusively within the territorial boundaries of the city of Federal Way.

Practice: The below practices will apply in the event that Federal Way Police Department (including SWAT or any other valley or combined unit) has reason to conduct a preplanned tactical operation at an address that is outside their primary jurisdiction.

A. Notification: Prior to initiating the operation, our assigned command level liaison will initiate contact with a command level officer at the agency with primary jurisdiction. These two command level officers will determine the appropriate assistance required from each agency which will be determined on a case-by-case basis. The intent of this procedure is to give the agency with primary jurisdiction:
• Notification of the preplanned tactical operation;
• Input into operational decisions occurring within their jurisdiction, and;
• An opportunity to provide information known to both agencies that may impact the safety of the officers involved in the operation.
The agency conducting the tactical operation will be responsible for the approval of all tactics and operational decisions related to the tactical operation.
B. Coordination: At a minimum, the following duties should be coordinated between the two agencies prior to the operation:
1. Determine which individual, by rank and name, will be designated the Incident Commander for the operation.
2. Assign a representative from both agencies to coordinate and ensure communications concerning the progress of the operation are made to both agencies in a timely fashion.
3. Determine which agency will be responsible for media inquiries concerning this operation.
4. Determine which agency will be primarily responsible for any follow-up investigation reference this operation.
5. Determine which agency will be responsible for traffic/crowd control at the scene of the operation, if needed.
6. Determine which radio channel to utilize while conducting the operation and which agency will be responsible for monitoring radio operations.
7. Discuss what additional resources from both agencies that may be required to safely conduct the tactical operation.

sections.title: HOMELAND SECURITY
paras: HOMELAND SECURITY PHILOSOPHY: The Federal Way Police Department recognizes the important role that municipal police agencies have in the security of our country. A critical part of our responsibilities is to help ensure the timely exchange of relevant information with the federal agencies tasked with coordinating a national effort. The practices provided in this section are intended to facilitate important communications.

sections.title: Homeland Security Liaison
paras: Principle: The SIU Lieutenant shall act as the central position for the Federal Way Police Department to receive and distribute information related to homeland security. They will primarily exchange information with the FBI Anti-Terrorism Task Force based in Seattle, but other avenues exist that can be used to disseminate this type of information. For example, the BDU Commander shares a bulletin relating to a bombing incident, which can provide relevant information to officers.

sections.title: Reporting Procedures
paras: Principle: Officers that receive or obtain information that may assist the FBI should provide the information to the SIU Lieutenant. However, if any officer receives or obtains information that they deem to be urgent they should contact the FBI directly.

sections.title: Community Awareness
paras: Principle: The Federal Way Police Department provides information to the community that assists citizens in identifying suspicious activity that may be related to terrorism.

sections.title: Hazardous Materials Awareness Training
paras: Principle: A hazardous materials response may result from various forms of incidents. The manner in which the Federal Way Police Department responds will have a direct bearing on the ability to control and defuse the incident as well as to control and contain property damage, injury, or loss of life.
Also reference 46.1.10 Hazardous Materials which outlines a detailed response to a hazardous materials incident

Practices – Prevention: Through high visibility patrol and proactive enforcement activities officers may be able to reduce the threat of the intentional use of hazardous materials in a criminal act within our community. They can not, however, eliminate accidents involving the legitimate, routine transportation and use of those materials on our roadways and in the community. Training in recognition, response procedures, and personal protective equipment will allow personnel to respond to a hazardous materials incident in a safe manner while reducing the threat to responders, the community and the environment. Responder training shall occur on an as needed basis in accordance with State and Federal guidelines for the number of hours, competency and content.

points.title: Use of Force — Philosophy
points.summary: FWPD states a belief in the sanctity of all human life and aims to deliver service with minimal reliance on physical force. Officers are expected to make split-second decisions; they must use only the degree of force reasonable under the circumstances as perceived at the time, to accomplish a legitimate law-enforcement purpose and bring the incident under control. De-escalation is used whenever the people, timing, and totality of circumstances allow. Voluntary compliance is described as the most effective de-escalation tool; where there is no resistance, no government compulsion is required. Officers are trained and equipped with non-lethal options, but the policy recognizes that no tactic works every time and that physical compulsion is sometimes necessary.
rules: Sanctity of all human life is the opening principle.
Use only the degree of force reasonable under the circumstances perceived at the time.
De-escalate whenever people, timing, and totality allow; compliance is the initial objective.
oral: How do you reconcile 'sanctity of all human life' with a deadly-force decision on a barricade or active assault?
What does 'voluntary compliance is our initial objective' mean on a high-risk warrant?
points.swat: This is the tone an oral board expects: life-first, force as a last effective means, comfort with non-lethal options, and no apology for using force when it is necessary. Footnote 14 in §4.4.1 later adds that 'all human life' includes responders, and that in lethal situations problem-causers get the lowest priority because they have the most power to stop the lethality.

points.title: Responding to Resistance — Authorization by Law (adopts RCW 10.120.020)
points.summary: FWPD adopts RCW 10.120.020 as policy. Physical force may be used only to the extent necessary for enumerated lawful purposes (protect against a crime with probable cause; effect an arrest; prevent escape under Ch. 9A.76 RCW; custody/transport under Ch. 10.77, 71.05, or 71.34 RCW; protective custody of a minor when authorized; execute/enforce a custody court order; execute a search warrant; execute a judicial directive that expressly authorizes force; stop a person actively fleeing a lawful Terry-type detention after notice that they are not free to leave; take a person into custody when authorized by statute; or protect against an imminent threat of bodily injury). Deadly force may be used only when necessary to protect against an immediate threat of serious physical injury or death, defined as an objectively reasonable belief, based on the totality of the circumstances, that the person has the present and apparent ability, opportunity, and intent to immediately cause death or serious bodily injury. Reasonable care requires: de-escalation tactics when possible; the least amount of physical force necessary to overcome resistance, considering listed characteristics (pregnancy, minor, vulnerable adult, impairment/disability, intoxication, suicidal, limited English, presence of children); terminating force when necessity ends; using available appropriate less-lethal alternatives before deadly force when possible; and making issued less-lethal tools reasonably available. Force tactics prohibited by policy or law may not be used except to protect the officer's life or another person's life from an imminent threat. The section does not limit lifesaving or community-caretaking functions, and does not authorize force that would violate the U.S. or state constitutions. When verbalization is feasible, one officer talking satisfies the verbalization/de-escalation communication principle for all on-scene officers.
rules: Physical force only to the extent necessary for a listed lawful purpose (RCW 10.120.020(1); MOS 4.1.1).
Deadly force only when necessary against an immediate threat — ability + opportunity + intent (RCW 10.120.020(2); MOS 4.1.1(2)).

Reasonable care: de-escalate when possible; least force necessary to overcome resistance; consider listed characteristics; terminate when necessity ends; less-lethal before deadly force when possible; keep issued less-lethal reasonably available (MOS 4.1.1(3)).
Prohibited tactics may be used only to protect life from an imminent threat (MOS 4.1.1(4); RCW 10.120.020(4)).
Footnote 1: 'possible' for de-escalation means feasible options for the situation.
Footnote 2: 'least amount' starts at something more than the subject's resisting effort; force that cannot overcome resistance may not be reasonable care.
thresholds: Deadly-force trigger: present and apparent ability, opportunity, and intent to immediately cause death or serious bodily injury.
Terry-flight force: only after notice that the person is being detained and is not free to leave (4.1.1(1)(i)).
oral: Recite the deadly-force standard including ability, opportunity, and intent.
List as many lawful purposes for physical force as you can, and give a SWAT example of one (search warrant, custody order, stopping flight from a detention).
What does 'necessary' plus 'least amount of force to overcome resistance' mean if a subject is still fighting after the first less-lethal round?
points.swat: This is the civil standard every V-SWAT use of force will be measured against in Washington, on top of Graham. Warrant service, entries, and less-lethal deployments must still map to a lawful purpose and to 'necessary.' The 'one communicator' rule matters on a call-out. The life-or-death exception in (4) is the same hook the department later uses for a last-resort vascular neck restraint (see 4.1.4 / 4.4.8 footnotes).

points.title: Definitions
points.summary: Thirty-two definitions apply throughout Chapter 4 unless context requires otherwise. The chapter expressly adopts or restates statutory definitions for chokehold, deadly force (treated as synonymous with lethal force), deadly weapon, de-escalation tactics, excessive force (for wrongdoing), immediate threat, less-lethal alternatives, neck restraint, peace officer, physical force, rifle (for 10.116.040), tear gas (CN, CS, and similar irritants; OC is excluded), totality of the circumstances, and wrongdoing. FWPD adds its own clarifying definitions for ability/opportunity/intent (not defined in the RCW or AG model), injury terms (serious bodily injury / serious physical harm / serious physical injury are equated to substantial bodily harm under RCW 9A.04.110), feasible, flight, proportional force (Graham factors, not 'the same as' the subject's force), reasonableness (Graham language quoted), and tool terms (CEW/ECW, PIW/IMS, non-lethal options vs. non-lethal weapons). Physical force does not include pat-downs, incidental touching, verbal commands, or compliant handcuffing with no pain or injury. Pointing a firearm and any weapon discharge (OC, CEW, firearm), hit or miss, are treated as force under 4.1.6, even though compliant handcuffing is excluded from 'physical force' here.
rules: Physical force (RCW 10.120.010(7)): an act reasonably likely to cause physical pain or injury, or any act on the body to compel/control/constrain/restrain movement — excluding pat-downs, incidental touching, verbal commands, and compliant handcuffing without pain or injury.
Totality of the circumstances (RCW 10.120.010(8)): all facts known to the officer leading up to and at the time of the force, including the person's actions and the officer's actions.
Tear gas (RCW 10.116.030(4)(d)): CN, CS, and similar airborne chemical irritants; does not include OC.

Immediate threat: objectively reasonable belief of present and apparent ability, opportunity, and intent to immediately cause death or serious bodily injury. FWPD defines ability (means), opportunity (proximity/access), and intent (what a reasonable officer may conclude the person is about to do).
Serious bodily injury, for deadly-force purposes in this policy, means the same as substantial bodily harm (temporary but substantial disfigurement or loss/impairment, or a fracture).
Proportional force considers the Graham factors and overcomes resistance without being excessive; it does not mean matching the subject's force.
thresholds: Substantial bodily harm includes a fracture of any bodily part (4.1.2(14)(f)).
Great bodily harm: probability of death, significant serious permanent disfigurement, or significant permanent loss/impairment.
oral: Does OC count as tear gas under Washington law?
Define immediate threat using ability, opportunity, and intent.
Is pointing a firearm 'physical force' under the statute, and is it reportable under FWPD policy?
points.swat: Memorize tear-gas vs. OC, the ability/opportunity/intent triad, and that totality includes the officer's own actions (this aligns with Barnes v. Felix). The physical-force definition matters for when a reportable 'use of force' starts (see also 4.1.6 and 4.1.11). Rifle and grenade definitions matter because RCW 10.116 restricts military equipment and rifles in some contexts; flash-bangs/stun grenades are excluded from the 'grenade' definition.
flags: Footnote 4 flags a 'conflicting perspective' between the general deadly-weapon definition (a vehicle can be a deadly weapon) and RCW 10.116.060(3) (a vehicle is not a deadly weapon for the shooting-at-vehicles rule unless the operator is using it as one and no other reasonable means to avoid serious harm are immediately available). Apply the vehicle-specific rule when the question is firing at a moving vehicle.

points.title: Additional Legal Authority
points.summary: In addition to RCW 10.120.020, officers must know and abide by RCW 9A.16.020, RCW 9A.16.040, Tennessee v. Garner, 471 U.S. 1 (1985), and Graham v. Connor, 490 U.S. 386 (1989). RCW 9A.16.020 is the criminal-law authorization for force necessarily used by a public officer in a legal duty (the policy quotes only part of the statute and tells members to read the rest). For deadly force / justifiable homicide, the policy says 10.120.020(2), 9A.16.040, and Garner all describe when deadly force may be considered, and that conflicting principles are resolved by deferring to RCW 10.120.020(2).
rules: Abide by 9A.16.020, 9A.16.040, Garner, and Graham in addition to 10.120.
If those authorities conflict, defer to RCW 10.120.020(2) on deadly force.
oral: If Garner, 9A.16.040, and RCW 10.120.020(2) seem to point different ways, which one does FWPD tell you to follow?
points.swat: Oral-board gold: you can explain the federal constitutional floor (Graham/Garner), the criminal statute (9A.16.040), and the stricter civil/operational standard (10.120.020(2)), and you know which one controls if they diverge.
flags: The policy does not reprint 9A.16.020 or 9A.16.040 in full; read the statutes themselves.

points.title: Chokehold or Neck Restraint Prohibited (adopts RCW 10.116.020)
points.summary: A peace officer may not use a chokehold or neck restraint in the course of duties. Chokehold: intentional direct pressure to the trachea or windpipe to restrict the airway. Neck restraint: any vascular neck restraint or similar tactic applying pressure to the neck to constrict blood flow. Agency policies must be consistent with the statute. Footnotes 11 and 16 (visually placed near 4.1.6 and 4.4.8 because of PDF layout) state FWPD's reading of RCW 10.120.020(4): because a life-or-death moment already justifies deadly force, a non-lethal VNR may be used to protect the officer or another person from an imminent threat of death or serious physical injury, and in that deadly-force context VNR is described as a life-saving de-escalation tactic.
rules: Chokeholds and neck restraints are prohibited in ordinary duties (RCW 10.116.020; MOS 4.1.4, 4.4.8).
FWPD footnote: VNR may be used only in a deadly-force / imminent-threat-to-life situation as a less-injurious alternative to shooting.
oral: Are neck restraints banned absolutely, or is there any exception in FWPD policy?
points.swat: Do not advertise VNR as a general control tool. If asked, state the ban first, then the narrow life-or-death reading in the footnotes, and be prepared to say you will follow how Valley SWAT trains it.
flags: The life-or-death VNR exception is in footnotes, not in the body of 4.1.4. Confirm current training doctrine before relying on it operationally.

points.title: Firing a Weapon Upon a Moving Vehicle (adopts RCW 10.116.060(3))
points.summary: An officer may not fire a weapon upon a moving vehicle unless necessary to protect against an imminent threat of serious physical harm resulting from the operator's or a passenger's use of a deadly weapon. A vehicle is not considered a deadly weapon unless the operator is using the vehicle as a deadly weapon and no other reasonable means to avoid potential serious harm are immediately available to the officer. Section 4.4.18 restates this and adds: when feasible, move out of the vehicle's path rather than shoot; do not shoot at any part of a vehicle to disable it; do not discharge a firearm from a moving vehicle unless a person is immediately threatening the officer or another with deadly force.
rules: No shooting at a moving vehicle except to stop an imminent serious-harm threat from a deadly weapon used by the operator or a passenger.
The vehicle itself counts as a deadly weapon only if used as one and no other reasonable means to avoid serious harm are immediately available.
Do not fire to disable a vehicle. Move out of the path when feasible (4.4.18).
oral: A driver is ramming patrol cars to escape. Can you shoot at the car to stop it? Walk through the 4.1.5 / 4.4.18 test.
points.swat: This is stricter than Scott v. Harris / Plumhoff federal law. A V-SWAT vehicle operation or a perimeter pursuit-related shooting will be judged under this statute and policy, not under Scott alone.
flags: Several later standards (4.2.2, 4.2.3, 41.1.4) still cross-reference 'Standard 4.1.5' for post-force / reporting practices. In this revision, firing-at-vehicles is 4.1.5 and post-force practices are 4.1.11. Treat those cross-references as stale numbering.

points.title: Other Force Concepts
points.summary: Force is broader than 'physical force.' It includes physical force, deadly force, and other compulsion/control that may not meet the statutory physical-force definition. Listed examples when intentionally used on or toward a person: handcuffing; physical strength (holding, grabbing, tackling, takedowns — not mere touching); counter-joint, pressure-point, and other pain compliance; strikes, including with impact or launching weapons; pointing a firearm directly at a person; and any discharge of OC, CEW, or a firearm, whether or not the person was hit. Ten additional 'force factors' supplement the reasonable-care characteristics in 4.1.1(3)(b): the subject's conduct as reasonably perceived; officer/subject factors (age, size, strength, skill, injury/exhaustion, numbers); drugs/alcohol and mental capacity; proximity of weapons; availability of other options; seriousness of the offense or reason for contact; officer training and experience; potential injury to citizens, officers, and suspects; risk of escape; and other exigent circumstances. Any employee who witnesses a Federal Way or outside-agency officer use force that appears to violate this standard must report it to a supervisor as soon as practical.
rules: Pointing a firearm at a person is a use of force.
Any weapon discharge (OC, CEW, firearm) is a use of force even if it misses.
Witnessed apparent policy-violating force, including by another agency, must be reported to a supervisor ASAP.
Ten force factors plus the 4.1.1(3)(b) characteristics guide reasonableness.
oral: Name as many of the 10 force factors as you can.
Is a missed CEW or a missed shot still a use of force?
points.swat: Muzzle discipline is a force decision, not just a safety habit. A pointed rifle on a call-out is reportable (see also 4.4.18 and RCW 10.118.030). The 10 factors are a ready-made articulation checklist for after-action and for the oral board.

points.title: Authorized Discharge of Firearm
points.summary: Besides authorized lethal force, a firearm may be discharged: (1) to kill a so-seriously-injured animal that humanity requires it, with prior supervisor approval and no other practical disposition; (2) to stop an animal that presents an imminent threat of injury to the officer or others; (3) for training or qualification at an approved range, or for lawful recreation.
rules: Humane dispatch of a suffering animal requires prior supervisor approval.
No other 'warning' or miscellaneous discharge authority is listed here.
oral: Can you shoot a mortally injured deer without calling a supervisor first?
points.swat: Low SWAT frequency, but a discharge toward an animal still triggers a Significant Incident email and a Discharge of a Firearm form (4.1.11). A discharge toward a person, hit or miss, requires a Use of Force form as well.

points.title: Warning Shots
points.summary: Warning shots are not authorized, because of extreme hazards to bystanders and citizens. Section 4.4.18 repeats: officers shall not fire a warning shot.
rules: Warning shots are prohibited. No exception is stated in 4.1.8 or 4.4.18.
oral: Are warning shots ever authorized?
points.swat: Absolute rule. Do not float a 'warning shot' as a de-escalation idea in an interview.

points.title: Non-Lethal Weapons
points.summary: Uniformed officers should always have two non-lethal weapons immediately accessible during enforcement activity (exempt while doing administrative tasks inside the PD). Prefer defensive-tactics techniques taught in training. OC will not be used on a handcuffed suspect unless the person still presents a threat to officers, themselves, or others. Only an authorized baton is the usual impact weapon; other immediate objects may be used in the manner prescribed if a baton is not immediately accessible. An impact weapon generally will not be used as a weapon against handcuffed or non-combative persons, except a handcuffed combative person who is not under control, when other options are ineffective and the officer reasonably believes the actions are necessary. Intentional lethal use of an impact weapon is allowed only when lethal force is authorized under 4.1.1(2). CEW is carried to be drawn with the non-dominant hand; should not be used on subjects exposed to flammable liquids (including alcohol-based pepper spray); should not be used on known pregnant females or elderly subjects unless options short of lethal force have failed or are inadvisable; cartridges will not be discharged at a person handcuffed behind the back unless the person is attempting to escape and escape would create an imminent public threat — a contact/drive-stun application may be used on a still-combative handcuffed subject. K-9 force is cross-referenced to 41.1.4. PIW (including 40mm): only after an instruction course, with refresher training every two years; the assigned PIW shall be accessible in the police vehicle each shift; if it is unavailable, notify a supervisor at the start of the shift. More PIW/ECW limits are in 4.4.17.
rules: Two non-lethal weapons immediately accessible on enforcement duty.
CEW on the support / non-dominant side to avoid a pistol draw confusion.
No OC on a handcuffed person unless they still present a threat.
PIW: trained, biennial refresher, accessible in the car, notify supervisor if missing.
thresholds: PIW refresher every two years.
CEW: support-hand draw in all but extreme circumstances (4.4.17).
oral: How do you carry a CEW and why?
When can you OC or baton a handcuffed person?
points.swat: 40mm / FN 303 / PIW are listed less-lethal tools in 4.4.16 and are classic SWAT and patrol-support tools. Carry and qualification rules still apply to you as a patrol officer and will apply on the team.
flags: 4.1.9 says PIWs are used 'in adherence to the restrictions listed below,' but in this extract the immediately following lines only address accessibility and a missing-weapon notification. Detailed PIW restrictions appear in 4.4.17. Possible page-break omission — do not assume 4.1.9 is the complete PIW rule set.

points.title: First Aid
points.summary: Officers shall provide or facilitate first aid at the earliest safe opportunity after any police action, at a scene controlled by law enforcement (RCW 36.28A.445). FWPD adopts the WSCJTC First Aid Guidelines: at the earliest safe opportunity, remove/control threats; request EMS; triage multiple injured (pulse, bleeding, breathing); provide aid to the level of training until a higher-trained person relieves you; use available medical resources (kits, AEDs, tourniquets); use PPE. Tool-specific aid: OC — flush eyes with clean water and ventilate with fresh air if possible; ECW — remove probes except in sensitive areas (head, female breast, groin), which an EMT or health professional must remove; treat probes as biohazard; canine bite that punctures skin — aid, request an aid unit, hospital treatment before booking.
rules: First aid at the earliest safe opportunity, not after paperwork.
Triage: pulse, bleeding, breathing.
Sensitive-area ECW probes stay in place for medical personnel.
Canine puncture: hospital before booking.
oral: You just CEW'd a subject and one probe is in the neck. What do you do?
Walk through first-aid priorities after a use of force.
points.swat: After a breach, less-lethal hit, or shooting, aid is a policy duty as soon as the scene is controlled enough to do it safely. This pairs with 46.1.11 (treat in place / CCP / rescue task force) and with TEMS if the team has it.

points.title: Other Post-Use of Force Practices (also CALEA 4.2.1)
points.summary: A force review process applies when an officer uses: any physical strength, skill, or pain compliance that results in visible injury or a complaint of injury; any physical strikes; any non-lethal weapon (the text cites 'Standard 4.1.4,' which in this revision is the chokehold section — likely a stale cross-reference to the non-lethal section now at 4.1.9); or any firearm discharge except departmental training or off-duty recreation. Medical aid is requested immediately for significant injury or loss of consciousness; offered for minor injury or complaint of injury. Report to the on-duty patrol supervisor as soon as practical after the incident is controlled; a supervisor should respond. The involved officer's supervisor completes a Use of Force Review with the officer (events, type of force, results, applicable directives) on the UOF Review form, routed within 10 calendar days (also Chapter 26). All involved officers write a supplement. A Significant Incident email goes out before end of shift. Humane animal dispatch: Significant Incident plus Discharge of a Firearm form; a UOF form is also completed whenever a firearm is discharged toward a person, even if the person is not hit. For force resulting in serious injury or death: call aid, notify a supervisor, try to apprehend outstanding suspects, find witnesses, protect the scene. The involved officer gives a brief verbal synopsis (public safety statement) and then limits further discussion. The first supervisor assumes the scene, obtains the public safety statement, notifies the commander (12.1.2), relieves involved officers and assigns a companion officer, leaves weapons on the ground as they lie when community safety allows, does not disarm officers at the scene of weapons still on their person, and when weapons are later collected the primary sidearm is immediately replaced. Involved officers may consult an attorney before a more detailed statement; the right may not unduly delay the statement. Peer support is contacted. After an OIS, a commander ensures an administrative round count of all FWPD officers in the immediate vicinity (all magazines for firearms present; locked-in-vehicle guns need not be counted). A mismatch, or an unlabeled magazine not loaded to capacity, means the officer is treated as a shooting officer until other evidence overcomes that assumption. Two investigations follow: a legal investigation (IIT/VIIT has primary jurisdiction when deadly force causes death, substantial bodily harm, or great bodily harm — RCW 10.114.011; WAC 139-12-020, 139-12-030) and an administrative review; the legal investigation takes precedence.
rules: UOF Review form with the supervisor within 10 calendar days.
Significant Incident email before end of shift.
Firearm discharged toward a person (hit or miss) = Use of Force form.
Public safety statement, then limit discussion; attorney consult before a detailed statement, without undue delay.
Do not disarm the officer at the scene of a holstered/slung weapon; replace a collected primary sidearm immediately.
OIS vicinity round count; IIT/VIIT has the legal investigation when death or substantial/great bodily harm results.
thresholds: 10 calendar days to route the UOF Review.
IIT trigger: death, substantial bodily harm, or great bodily harm from deadly force or other officer actions.
oral: What do you say in a public safety statement, and what do you not discuss?
Who investigates an officer-involved shooting that causes serious injury?
points.swat: Know your role as an involved officer versus a first arriving supervisor versus a teammate/companion officer. Round-count and weapon-handling discipline after a shooting will be expected of SWAT operators. Do not contaminate the IIT interview.
flags: 4.1.11's non-lethal-weapon trigger cites 'Standard 4.1.4,' which is now the chokehold section. The non-lethal section is 4.1.9. Flag as a stale cross-reference.
IIT process details are referred to the VIIT Organization and Operational Manual and to Chapter 52, which were not in the provided docs.
cites: FWPD MOS Ch. 26 and Ch. 52 (referenced, not in the provided docs)

points.title: Reporting, Review, Leave, Annual Analysis, Assault-on-Officer Review
points.summary: 4.2.1 (Reporting) is a one-line referral (it cites 4.1.5; the actual reporting practice is in 4.1.11). 4.2.2: all Use of Force Reports go to the Chief or designee and to Professional Standards for ongoing analysis; the analysis looks at similar characteristics, department policy, and training, with recommendations as needed (also refers to 4.2.4). 4.2.3: if an employee's official actions cause death or serious physical injury, the employee is placed on administrative leave or operational reassignment, without loss of pay or benefits, pending investigation; this is not an implication of wrongdoing. The Chief may order a psychological debriefing and, case-by-case, a fitness-for-duty exam. 4.2.4 is a one-line referral to 4.2.2. 4.2.5: assaults on officers are reviewed because they significantly affect public-safety-personnel safety.
rules: UOF reports to the Chief and Professional Standards.
Death or serious injury caused in an official capacity → paid admin leave or reassignment; not a finding of fault.
oral: If you are in a fatal shooting, what happens to your assignment and pay, and what does that leave mean?
points.swat: Expect to be taken off the line after a serious-force event. That is policy, not punishment.
flags: 4.2.1, 4.2.2, and 4.2.3 still refer to Standard 4.1.5 for reporting/post-force practices. In this revision those practices live in 4.1.11.

points.title: Authorized Weapons and Ammunition
points.summary: Officers are issued no more than one pistol and no more than one long gun. The SWAT Commander may authorize additional weapons for SWAT officers when necessary to fulfill the team's goals and objectives, following the approval process in this standard. Only department-approved and issued ammunition may be carried or used in a law-enforcement capacity. The section also covers the approval process, unsafe-firearm practices, weapon security, taking an issued long gun off-site for personal practice, carrying firearms out of state and LEOSA limits, records kept by the firearms-training commander, former-officer LEOSA qualifications, and privately owned firearms (the officer pays for and retains them, subject to authorization rules).
rules: Patrol issue: one pistol, one long gun, unless SWAT command authorizes more for team members.
Only approved/issued ammunition in a law-enforcement capacity.
oral: How many long guns may a patrol officer be issued, and who can authorize more?
points.swat: This is the written hook for SWAT-specific weapons beyond standard patrol issue. The approval process still runs through this standard. Do not assume a team weapon is automatically authorized for off-duty or patrol carry.
flags: The body of 4.3.1 is long (authorized models, security, LEOSA). This outline does not inventory every approved firearm model. Read 4.3.1 in full before a weapons-board or armorer's question.

points.title: Weapon Proficiency, Training and Qualification, Carry Rules, Firearms Range
points.summary: Only officers who demonstrate proficiency may carry those weapons. Initial training must be by a currently certified instructor and includes use-of-force / lethal-force law and policy and safe handling; documentation is kept at least six years after separation. Before on-duty or color-of-authority off-duty carry, the officer must demonstrate proficiency to a certified instructor (minimum qualifying scores and knowledge of law/policy). A non-probationary officer who fails the primary service-pistol proficiency test is not entirely disarmed; the assignment is temporarily modified to reduce public contact and eliminate contact with suspected violators. At least annually, all officers authorized to carry firearms receive in-service training on use-of-force policies and demonstrate proficiency with all approved lethal weapons and ECWs they are authorized to use. Non-lethal weapons and weaponless control techniques: at least biennially. CEW annual proficiency includes loading, unloading, deploying, and accurately discharging the prongs. Remedial training is given if time allows; no more than five qualification attempts on a single day. Authorization is suspended until proficiency is shown (with the primary-pistol exception above). The FTU offers at least one optional unpaid open range day per year with practice ammunition. 4.3.4: officers authorized to carry a lethal or non-lethal weapon shall be issued a copy of Chapter 4 and demonstrate knowledge (via 12.2.1 / Written Directives System). 4.3.5 sets range protocols for FWPD practice.
rules: Annual UOF-policy training and annual proficiency for firearms and ECW.
Biennial in-service for non-lethal weapons and weaponless control (4.3.3); defensive tactics also annual under 4.4.21.
Max five qualification attempts in one day.
Failed primary-pistol qual (non-probationary): not fully disarmed; assignment modified.
thresholds: Annual firearms/ECW proficiency.
Biennial non-lethal / weaponless in-service under 4.3.3; annual DT under 4.4.21.
Five qual attempts per day.
Training records retained at least six years after separation.
oral: How often must you qualify with a CEW? With a baton?
What happens if you fail pistol qualification?
points.swat: Selection itself includes a shooting qualification (46.2.2). An annual patrol qual is the floor, not the team standard. If you are unqualified on a weapon, you may not carry it under department authority.
flags: 4.3.3 says non-lethal and weaponless training at least biennially; 4.4.21 says defensive-tactics training occurs annually. Those can both be true (DT annual satisfies 'at least biennial'), but do not collapse them into one interval without reading both.

points.title: Preserve Life; De-escalate; Reasonable Care; Terminate Force; Necessary and Lawful; Warnings
points.summary: 4.4 restates duties in AG-model style. 4.4.1: the fundamental duty is to preserve and protect all human life (RCW 10.120.010). Footnote 14: 'all human life' includes responders; in potentially lethal situations, people with the least power to end the conflict (e.g., children in a school with an armed aggressor) get the highest priority, and problem-causers the lowest, because they can immediately cease lethality. 4.4.2: when possible, use all available and appropriate de-escalation tactics before physical force (time, distance, cover, communication). 4.4.3: consider listed characteristics when deciding whether and how much force to use (minors or presence of children, pregnancy, vulnerable adult, impaired/disabled, alcohol/drugs, limited English). 4.4.4: terminate physical force as soon as necessity ends. 4.4.5: physical force shall be necessary and for a lawful purpose. Necessary means a reasonably effective alternative does not appear to exist and the force must be a reasonable and proportional response. Reasonableness is totality-based; proportionality tracks immediacy and severity of the threat or resistance and the seriousness of the objective; the threat may change during the incident; proportional does not mean the same type or amount of force; the more immediate and likely the death/serious-injury threat, the greater the level of force that may be proportional. 4.4.6 lists lawful purposes (similar to 4.1.1, and also lists 'execute any other community caretaking function'). 4.4.7: when safe and feasible, before physical force, identify as police, try to determine if a condition may affect understanding, give clear instructions and a warning that force will be used unless resistance ceases, and give a reasonable opportunity to comply.
rules: Necessary = no reasonably effective alternative appears to exist, and the force is reasonable and proportional (4.4.5).
Proportional ≠ the same as. It tracks threat immediacy/severity and the objective, using Graham factors (n.15).
When safe and feasible: ID, assess ability to comply, warn, give a reasonable chance to comply (4.4.7).
Terminate force when necessity ends.
oral: Define 'necessary' as FWPD uses it in 4.4.5.
When would you not give a warning before force?
points.swat: 4.4.1 n.14 is a clean way to talk about active-assault priorities (stop the killing; victims first). 4.4.7 warnings matter on a call-out 'when safe and feasible' — they are not a suicide pact on an active killer.
flags: 4.4.6 lists 'execute any other community caretaking function' as a lawful purpose for physical force. 4.1.1 / RCW 10.120.020(5) say the statute does not limit lifesaving or community-caretaking, but caretaking is not one of the enumerated physical-force purposes in 4.1.1(1). Do not treat caretaking as a blank check for force; stay inside 4.1.1(1) plus the life-saving language in 4.1.1(5).
4.4.3's characteristic list is shorter than 4.1.1(3)(b) (it omits 'suicidal' in the 4.4.3 bullets). Use the fuller 4.1.1 list when articulating reasonable care.

points.title: Neck Restraints; Duty to Intervene; First Aid; Asphyxia; ECW Probes; Least Force; Head Strikes
points.summary: 4.4.8 restates the chokehold/neck-restraint ban, with the same life-or-death VNR footnote. 4.4.9: any identifiable on-duty officer who witnesses another officer engaging or attempting to engage in excessive force shall intervene when in a position to do so; any identifiable on-duty officer who witnesses any wrongdoing shall report it to a supervisor (RCW 10.93.190). 4.4.10 restates first aid (RCW 36.28A.445) and says personnel may monitor injured and restrained persons in custody. 4.4.11 asphyxia-risk reduction: roll the person to the side and to an upright position that does not impede breathing, except if unconscious; do not put prolonged pressure on the chest, neck, or back (including sitting, kneeling, or standing); continuously monitor breathing, color, and verbalized impairment; designate a Safety Officer when possible; do not transport a person in the prone position. 4.4.12: ECW probes in sensitive areas (head, breast, groin) are removed only by an EMT, paramedic, or other health professional. 4.4.13: least amount of physical force necessary to overcome resistance under the circumstances then known (footnote 17 repeats the 'least amount starts above the subject's effort' idea). 4.4.14: striking techniques directed at the head only as self-defense or defense of others; intentional head strikes with fists, elbows, knees, and feet shall not be used as pain compliance.
rules: Duty to intervene in excessive force when in a position to do so; duty to report wrongdoing (4.4.9; RCW 10.93.190).
No prolonged pressure on chest/neck/back; no prone transport; use a Safety Officer when possible (4.4.11).
No head strikes as pain compliance (4.4.14).
Unconscious exception to the 'roll to the side / upright' instruction (4.4.11) — treat as a medical/positioning issue, not a reason to leave someone face-down under pressure.
oral: A teammate is kneeling on a prone subject's back after the fighting has stopped. What is your duty?
May you use a closed-fist strike to the head to get a handcuffed subject to spit out contraband?
points.swat: After a takedown or a piled-on arrest at a warrant, the Safety Officer and no-prone-transport rules are life-safety and oral-board material. Intervention is a statutory duty, not optional loyalty.
flags: 4.4.9 states the intervene/report duties but, unlike some earlier study notes, this revision's 4.4.9 text does not itself include a '30-second' timing rule. If a 30-second figure appears in training or another directive, it is not in this 4.4.9 paragraph.

points.title: Deadly Force, Less-Lethal Menu and Limits, Firearms
points.summary: 4.4.15: use deadly force only when necessary to protect against an immediate threat of serious physical injury or death; do not use deadly force against persons who present a danger only to themselves; whenever possible, use available appropriate less-lethal alternatives first. Deadly force includes: intentional impact-weapon strikes to the head, neck, throat, or spine; intentionally striking a person's head into a hard, fixed object; discharging a firearm loaded with lethal ammunition at a person; and intentionally striking with a vehicle a person who is not inside a vehicle. 4.4.16 lists less-lethal tools: TASER (ECW), OC, ASP or wooden baton, 40mm launcher, FN 303, and personal impact weapons (hands, feet, elbows, knees). 4.4.17: each subsequent OC application must be justified; no intentional impact-weapon strikes to vital areas (head, neck, face, throat, spine, groin, kidney) unless deadly force is authorized; do not warn that an impact weapon may be used if its use is not justified; reassess impact strikes and change target or tactic if ineffective. PIW: trained before deploy; assess after each shot; do not intentionally aim at head, neck, chest, or groin, use ranges inconsistent with manufacturer guidelines, or engage a person on an elevated surface (unless reasonable efforts to prevent a fall injury) unless deadly force is justified. ECW: carry when uniformed or on enforcement activity; support-side, support-hand except in extreme circumstances; avoid head, neck, chest, genitals; drive-stun primarily to complete a circuit; one standard cycle of five seconds or less, then reassess; minimum cycles; after three ineffective cycles, assume the ECW may not be working and consider other options; articulate each application. Do not use ECW on a fleeing person absent other factors; on a handcuffed/restrained person unless deadly force is authorized (note some tension with 4.1.9's contact-stun allowance for a combative handcuffed subject); on an elevated surface without fall mitigation; on an operator in physical control of a moving vehicle unless deadly force is authorized; or where flammable/volatile/explosive material is present. 4.4.18: discharge a firearm at a person only when deadly force is authorized; each discharge must be justified; pointing a firearm at a person is a reportable use of force and must be reported to the statewide UOF data program (RCW 10.118.030); verbal warning that a firearm will be discharged when feasible; no firearm-as-impact-weapon unless deadly force is permitted or to keep a resisting person from taking the weapon; moving-vehicle rule as in 4.1.5; move out of the path when feasible; do not shoot to disable a vehicle; do not fire from a moving vehicle unless a person is immediately threatening with deadly force; do not fire when it appears likely an innocent person may be injured; no warning shots; do not discharge or point a firearm at a person who is a danger only to themselves without ability/opportunity/intent to immediately harm the officer or another, or who is a danger only to property.
rules: No deadly force against a person who is a danger only to themselves (4.4.15, 4.4.18).
Deadly force includes certain head/neck/spine impact strikes, driving a vehicle into a person not in a vehicle, and firing lethal ammunition at a person.
ECW: ≤5-second standard cycle, reassess; after three cycles if still aggressing, consider other options.
Pointing a firearm at a person is reportable (RCW 10.118.030).
Each firearm discharge must be separately justified.
thresholds: ECW standard cycle: five seconds or less.
ECW decision point: three applications.
oral: A barricaded man has a gun to his own head and is not threatening anyone else. May you shoot him to 'stop the threat to himself'?
When does a 40mm round to the chest become a deadly-force problem?
After three CEW cycles the subject is still fighting. What does policy tell you to consider?
points.swat: The 'danger only to themselves' rule is central to barricaded suicidal subjects. Less-lethal (40mm, FN 303, ECW) is how you try to solve that without violating 4.4.15. Innocent-person risk is why you do not take low-percentage shots through walls or across a hostage.
flags: 4.4.17 says an ECW should not be used on a handcuffed or otherwise restrained person unless deadly force is authorized. 4.1.9 allows a contact CEW application to gain compliance from a handcuffed subject who remains combative, and allows a cartridge discharge only if the handcuffed-behind-the-back person is attempting escape and escape would create an imminent public threat. There is tension between these two sections. Flag it and default to the more restrictive reading unless current training resolves it: do not cartridge-deploy a CEW on a restrained person unless the 4.1.9 escape/imminent-threat facts (or deadly force) are present.

points.title: Spit Guards, Hobble Restraints, Training, Canine Team Policies
points.summary: 4.4.19: only agency-issued spit guards; warn and give reasonable time to comply before applying; fasten for adequate ventilation; remove as soon as the spit/bite threat ends or the guard is no longer necessary; do not apply if the person is bleeding profusely around the mouth/nose, is actively vomiting (remove and discard if they vomit while wearing it), or has a medical condition affecting breathing or shows labored/distressed breathing; after application, move to a seated or side-recovery position and monitor until removal; assist while escorting because of impaired vision; document; discard after each use. 4.4.20: only agency-issued hobbles; do not 'hog-tie' (do not connect a hobble to rear handcuffs); once applied, do not place the person face down; monitor and protect health; discontinue when necessity ends. 4.4.21: defensive-tactics training annually for commissioned and limited-commission employees; this policy should be in the DT curriculum. 4.4.22 is a long canine-team force policy (handler evaluation of totality, including under E2SHB 1310 / RCW 10.120). Patrol officers need the intersections: K-9 is a force option (4.1.9 points to 41.1.4); a bite that punctures skin requires aid, an aid unit, and hospital care before booking (4.1.10).
rules: No hog-tying; no face-down after a hobble; no prone transport (4.4.11 + 4.4.20).
Spit guard: warn first, monitor, seated or side recovery, never on a vomiting or distressed-breathing subject.
Annual DT training (4.4.21).
oral: May you connect a hobble to rear handcuffs?
A spitting subject starts vomiting into a spit guard. What do you do?
points.swat: Hobble/spit-guard and asphyxia rules apply to everyone who takes a prisoner into custody after a warrant or barricade surrender. Canine is often a SWAT/perimeter asset; know when a bite becomes a medical event.
flags: 4.4.22 is lengthy and handler-specific. This study set does not treat you as a K-9 handler. Read 4.4.22 and 41.1.4 in full if a board question goes deep on canine deployments.

points.title: Patrol Shift Management, Briefings, Special Purpose Vehicles
points.summary: FWPD provides 24/7 patrol coverage. The Chief may call an officer back to duty (Guild contract Arts. 2 and 8). Shift bidding is by seniority (Art. 7); the Chief may reassign with cause; shift trades need deputy-chief approval. Sector assignments are made by the squad supervisor with shift-commander approval, considering experience, specialty skills (the policy expressly lists FTO and SWAT among examples), productivity, and officer safety; seniority preferences are gathered but are not controlling. Sector assignments are generally annual to support community policing. Minimum staffing: 7 officers midnight to 1400; 9 officers 1400 to midnight. Traffic and K-9 may count toward minimum staffing; contract-services positions may not. Lieutenants may operate below minimum for short periods (1–2 hours) during unanticipated shortages. 41.1.2: shift briefings exchange information (crime, BOLOS, training, inspections — details in the standard). 41.1.3: special-purpose vehicles exist; the standard refers to a Special Purpose Vehicle table/section rather than listing them all here.
rules: Minimum staffing 7 (0000–1400) and 9 (1400–0000).
SWAT skill is a listed factor in sector assignment.
Below-minimum staffing only for short unanticipated periods (1–2 hours) at a lieutenant's discretion.
thresholds: Staffing floors: 7 / 9 officers by time of day.
Below-minimum window: 1–2 hours.
oral: What is FWPD's patrol minimum staffing, and who may go below it?
points.swat: Your SWAT assignment can affect patrol-sector placement. Know the staffing floor because a major call (barricade, active assault) will immediately stress it and drive a Phase I/II mobilization (Ch. 46).
flags: Guild-contract articles are referenced, not reproduced. Shift-trade and callback details live in the contract.

points.title: Canine (K-9) Unit
points.summary: A long, specialized standard covering K-9 missions, definitions, deployment practices, handler responsibilities, use of force with a dog, post-bite procedures, and audits. 4.1.9 directs officers to this standard when a K-9 is used as force. 4.1.10 requires aid, an aid unit, and hospital treatment before booking for any canine bite that punctures skin. This chapter also notes that a request for neighboring-agency K-9 help is not, by itself, a Phase II mobilization under 46.1.2.
rules: K-9 is a force option governed by 41.1.4 and Chapter 4.
Puncture bite: aid + hospital before booking (4.1.10).
Neighbor K-9 assist ≠ automatic Phase II (46.1.2).
oral: A SWAT call-out dog bites a suspect who then surrenders. What medical steps are required?
points.swat: K-9 is a common perimeter, tracking, and call-out asset. Know how to request it and what medical follow-up is mandatory after a bite.
flags: 41.1.4 is long and handler-centric. This outline is not a handler's manual. One internal cross-reference in 41.1.4 points to 'standard 4.1.5 (Post Use of Force Practices)'; those practices are in 4.1.11 in the May 2026 Ch. 4.

points.title: Operations of Police Vehicles (priority / routine response)
points.summary: Governed by RCW 46.61.035 and the Federal Way municipal code. Routine response: obey all traffic laws; no lights and siren. Priority response: continuous emergency lights and siren while operating contrary to traffic regulations; only department police officers may drive in priority mode. Priority is authorized for: officer needs assistance (Code 2 or Code 3 — definitions are in MOS 81.2.5, not in this document); calls involving seriously injured persons or imminent threat to life or serious bodily injury; collisions with a probable report of a seriously injured person; felony crimes in progress; or when a supervisor authorizes it (the officer remains responsible for safe operation). Notify dispatch when practical that you are responding priority. Hazard lights shall not be activated in priority mode; do not spotlight oncoming windshields. Terminate priority as soon as circumstances allow; you may deactivate warning devices at a distance from the scene for a stealthy approach and continue routine. Officers are not compelled to continue a priority response when roadway, weather, traffic, or vehicle conditions make it unsafe. Vehicle classes: fully marked emergency-equipped cars may do all authorized emergency operations; prisoner vans, some unequipped vehicles, and unequipped unmarked cars have limits; fully equipped unmarked cars may be used in priority mode when driven by a police officer. Emergency escorts of civilian vehicles are referred to 61.3.3.
rules: Priority response = lights and siren on continuously.
Authorized: officer assistance Code 2/3; serious injury or imminent serious-injury/life threat; serious-injury collisions; in-progress felonies; supervisor authorization.
You may always slow or drop to routine for safety. A supervisor's authorization does not remove your duty of safe operation.
oral: When are you authorized to run priority, and when should you turn the siren off before arrival?
points.swat: This is how you get to a barricade, hostage, or active assault. 'Felony in progress' and 'imminent threat to life' cover most SWAT-activation calls. Stealth approach (drop to routine near the scene) is written into policy and is often the right last mile.
flags: Code 2 and Code 3 definitions are in MOS 81.2.5, which was not provided.

points.title: Vehicular Pursuits
points.summary: The policy adopts the RCW 10.116.060(5) definition of a vehicular pursuit (uniformed officer, emergency-equipped vehicle, suspect appears aware of the stop signal and willfully resists by speeding, evasive maneuvers, or reckless driving that endangers the community or the officer). It is not a pursuit if the violator slows and appears to be looking for a place to stop. Only general-commission officers who meet all of these may drive in a pursuit: EVOC in the last 24 months including ongoing risk-analysis training; trained and authorized in at least one intervention technique (tire deflation or PIT); wearing a police uniform; driving an emergency-equipped police vehicle (some specialty vehicles are barred). FWPD's authorized reasons to pursue are narrower than the current statute: reasonable suspicion or probable cause that the driver or occupants have committed or are about to commit a felony, or DUI under RCW 46.61.502. Eluding alone is not enough to start, authorize, or continue a pursuit. Upon initiation, immediately notify a field supervisor/commander, who must maintain continued oversight; as soon as practicable, develop a plan to end the pursuit with an approved technique; constantly reassess. Terminate if: the danger outweighs the need for apprehension (primary officer, supervisor, or commander may decide); the suspect is identified and later apprehension can be accomplished without an immediate need; traffic, roadway, or environmental conditions make continued pursuit futile; or the pursued vehicle's location is no longer known. On termination, turn off emergency equipment and obey the rules of the road. Vehicle limits: fully marked cars may pursue; marked motorcycles may initiate but must yield to four-wheeled marked cars ASAP (dual-sport motorcycles may not initiate or participate); unmarked emergency-equipped cars may initiate but must yield to marked cars ASAP. Banned from pursuing: vehicles without lights and siren; prisoner van; dual-sport and unmarked motorcycles; auxiliary vehicles including the evidence van, bomb truck, and SWAT truck; animal-services trucks; a vehicle actively transporting a prisoner. Normally up to three police vehicles; more may be authorized based on number of suspects, reason to believe they are armed, the threat to life, or when PIT is authorized. Lights and siren stay on the entire time a unit is in the pursuit or operating emergency due to it. Primary unit must radio unit ID, that they are in a pursuit, the crime, location/speed/direction, and vehicle description/plate; failure to provide this may cause a supervisor to terminate. Secondary unit handles radio when needed, stays back, does not intersect the path. Other units maintain radio silence except for mission-critical information (including tire-deflation deployment), may clear intersections or respond for a post-pursuit perimeter, and shall not violate the rules of the road to parallel on adjacent streets.
rules: FWPD may pursue only for a felony or DUI — not for eluding alone (41.2.2.B).
Current RCW 10.116.060 (I-2113, 2024 c 6) is broader (reasonable suspicion of a law violation plus necessity and a risk-balance test). FWPD policy is stricter; follow the policy.
Driver qualifications: EVOC within 24 months (with risk-analysis training), certified in at least one intervention tactic, uniformed, in an authorized emergency-equipped vehicle.
Immediate supervisor notification and continued oversight; plan to end the pursuit ASAP.
SWAT truck, bomb truck, prisoner van, and a unit transporting a prisoner may not pursue.
Normally max three police vehicles.
thresholds: EVOC currency: 24 months.
Default pursuit vehicles: up to three.
PIT above 40 mph requires the monitoring supervisor's authorization (41.2.3).
oral: A car runs from a traffic stop and the only crime so far is eluding. Do you pursue? Why or why not?
Is FWPD pursuit policy the same as the current RCW after Initiative 2113?
May the SWAT truck join a pursuit?
points.swat: A felony-suspect flight from a warrant or a perimeter can become a pursuit. Know that the SWAT truck is not a pursuit vehicle, that eluding is not enough under FWPD policy, and that federal cases (Scott, Plumhoff) do not authorize a Washington/FWPD pursuit by themselves.
flags: IMPORTANT POLICY/STATUTE GAP: After Initiative 2113 (2024 c 6), RCW 10.116.060(1) allows a pursuit when there is reasonable suspicion the person violated the law, the pursuit is necessary to identify or apprehend, the person poses a threat to the safety of others, and the risks of not apprehending outweigh the risks of the pursuit, plus supervisor and training conditions. FWPD 41.2.2.B (revised 12-08-2025, after I-2113) still limits authorized reasons to felony or DUI and says eluding alone is insufficient. Agencies may be stricter than the statute. Follow 41.2.2 unless and until the department amends it. If a board or a supervisor frames the question as 'what does the RCW allow,' distinguish the statute from the policy.

points.title: Pursuit Tactics (PIT, boxing-in, tire deflation, roadblocks)
points.summary: PIT is intentional forced rotational contact to stop a fleeing vehicle. It is discretionary, is not 'ramming,' and the contact is not documented as a collision. At 40 mph and under it is available to officers who have completed the prescribed course. Consider site (level, exit path, limited roadside obstructions), oncoming traffic and pedestrians, vehicle type (high-center / oversized-tire / 4x4 vehicles only after other methods are considered, because of rollover risk), and multiple occupants. PIT over 40 mph requires authorization from the supervisor monitoring the pursuit, and may be used when the totality requires immediate intervention. Officers will not be disciplined for deciding not to PIT. Boxing-in requires supervisor or commander approval, and may be used only if there is no reason to believe the fleeing person is armed with a firearm; officers shall not intentionally cause contact during boxing-in. Tire-deflation devices require supervisor authorization; notify pursuing units of the deployment location. Forcible stopping (ramming, forcing a vehicle off the road or into obstacles) is prohibited unless specifically approved by the supervisor or commander and only in circumstances justifying deadly force. Roadblocks likewise require deadly-force-level circumstances and supervisor approval; personnel stay a safe distance from blocking vehicles; the site must be visible with emergency lights/flares/cones; pursuing units give the suspect room to slow. No passing other police units in the pursuit without permission from the primary unit or supervisor. Maintain spacing. Do not pursue the wrong way on interstate, other controlled-access, or any divided highway. Extreme caution at signals: slow and proceed only when approaching vehicles have yielded. Training on roadblocks and authorized tactics is as-needed. Pursuits are reported and administratively reviewed.
rules: PIT ≤40 mph: trained officers; PIT >40 mph: monitoring supervisor must authorize.
No discipline for declining to PIT.
Boxing-in: supervisor/commander approval, and not if you have reason to believe the person is armed with a firearm; no intentional contact.
Tire deflation: supervisor authorization.
Ramming / forcing off the road, and physical roadblocks: only if deadly force is justified, and with supervisor/commander approval.
No wrong-way pursuit on interstates, controlled-access, or divided highways.
thresholds: PIT supervisor threshold: speeds above 40 mph.
oral: When can you PIT above 40 mph?
May you box in a car if the passenger is reported to have a gun?
Is a roadblock a use of deadly force under this policy?
points.swat: Ramming and roadblocks are deadly-force tactics. A vehicle-assault or high-risk stop on a warrant flight has to meet 4.4.15 / 10.120.020(2) as well as this section. Boxing-in is off the table if the suspect is believed to have a firearm — a common SWAT fact pattern.

points.title: Notifications; Missing Persons; Juvenile Missing Persons
points.summary: 41.2.4 covers notification practices when FWPD operations depend on other agencies or resources (details in the standard). 41.2.5–41.2.6 are detailed missing-person and missing-juvenile investigation standards, including database entries and AMBER / Blue Alert criteria (Blue Alert criteria are tied to RCW 10.108.030). A missing/trapped person who may need search-and-rescue ties to 46.2.5.
rules: Missing-person and AMBER/Blue Alert processes are mandatory investigative standards, not optional.
SAR requests go through the on-duty supervisor and King County processes (46.2.5).
thresholds: AMBER activation should occur within 4 hours of a qualifying event (language in 41.2.6).
oral: If a barricade starts as a 'missing endangered' call, who do you notify besides SWAT?
points.swat: Lower direct SWAT frequency, except when a missing-person or abduction call becomes a barricade, hostage, or tracking/K-9 operation.
flags: These sections are long. This outline does not attempt a complete AMBER/Blue Alert checklist; read 41.2.5–41.2.6 if that is a board topic.

points.title: Responding to Persons with Mental Health Issues
points.summary: Patrol will routinely contact people with mental-health issues. The standard covers recognition, response practices, and involuntary custody. RCW 71.05.150(4) allows a peace officer to take a person into custody for evaluation under stated criteria. RCW 9A.16.020 is cited for the use of force to prevent a mentally ill person from committing a dangerous act (as always, still constrained by Ch. 4 and RCW 10.120). Officers may assist a mental-health professional's investigation (RCW 71.05.157). A person taken into custody under these authorities should be processed as expeditiously as practicable. These contacts often also trigger the reasonable-care characteristics in 4.1.1(3)(b) and 4.4.3 (impairment, disability, suicidal, presence of children).
rules: Mental-health authority to take a person into custody is statutory (Ch. 71.05 / 71.34 / 10.77) and is also a listed lawful purpose for physical force in 4.1.1.
Force during these contacts still must be necessary, proportional, and consistent with Chapter 4.
Deadly force is not authorized against a person who is a danger only to themselves (4.4.15, 4.4.18).
oral: An armed, suicidal subject will not come out but has not pointed the gun at anyone else. What lawful purposes and what force limits apply?
points.swat: Many barricades are crisis/mental-health events, not hostage crimes. Your first-arriving job is contain, slow down, call resources (including Crisis Communications / DCR), and avoid turning a self-harm crisis into a deadly-force event.
flags: 41.2.7 is long. Confirm current ITA / DCR procedures; statutes are amended periodically. Do not recite commitment criteria from memory without checking the current RCW if a board goes deep.

points.title: Domestic Violence; Electronic Recording of Custodial Interrogation
points.summary: 41.2.8 (WASPC 15.7) is FWPD's DV-response standard, including arrest-authority references to RCW 10.31.100. 41.2.9 (WASPC 2.8 and 2.9) makes it policy to protect constitutional rights of suspects and to record custodial interrogations. Miranda is required when there is custodial interrogation and/or after formal arrest. Juvenile waiver of rights is tied to RCW 13.40.140. Misconduct captured on a recording is disciplined the same as misconduct that is not recorded.
rules: DV: follow 41.2.8 and RCW 10.31.100 arrest rules.
Custodial interrogation is recorded per 41.2.9; Miranda applies to custodial interrogation and/or after formal arrest.
oral: You take a barricaded DV suspect into custody. When must Miranda and recording occur?
points.swat: DV and family-violence calls are a common path into barricade/hostage situations. After a warrant or a surrender, any custodial interview of the suspect should follow 41.2.9.
flags: 41.2.8–41.2.9 are detailed operational standards; this is a study-level summary, not a complete DV checklist.

points.title: Patrol Vehicles, Equipment, Restraints, Apparel, MDC, AVL
points.summary: Patrol vehicles used for general patrol are equipped with emergency lights and a siren consistent with RCW 46.61.035 and 46.37.190, plus at least one spotlight. 41.3.2 covers required vehicle equipment, inspection, and replenishment. 41.3.3: all members use vehicle safety restraints in compliance with state law and city guidelines (details in the standard). 41.3.4: authorized personal equipment and apparel are limited to the Authorized Equipment and Apparel Table; practices for carrying unapproved gear are in the standard. 41.3.7: MDC use and practices. 41.3.9: AVL shows the location of each equipped vehicle for safety and dispatch efficiency. There is no Standard 41.3.6 in this document.
rules: Only authorized equipment and apparel.
Seat belts per 41.3.3.
AVL is an officer-safety and dispatch tool, not optional decoration.
oral: May you install personally bought unapproved equipment on a patrol car or uniform?
points.swat: Lower oral-board frequency except: do not add unapproved tactical gear to a patrol uniform, and know that the SWAT truck is a special-purpose / auxiliary vehicle with pursuit limits (41.2.2).
flags: No 41.3.6 appears in the provided chapter (numbering jumps 41.3.5 to 41.3.7). The vest standard is numbered 41.3.5 and annotated 'CALEA 41.3.6.'

points.title: Protective Vests
points.summary: The department issues protective vests to all officers. For non-uniformed officers, wear is optional except: when serving a search and/or arrest warrant; when engaging in any enforcement action; when contacting a criminal suspect; or when a commissioned supervisor directs it. Formal dress: vest optional, and if worn must be concealed. Class A and Class B: vest shall be worn and concealed under the shirt. Field uniforms (patrol jumpsuit, bicycle, motorcycle): vest shall be worn, either concealed or as an external carrier that meets this policy. Officers must maintain a concealment carrier and a complete patrol duty belt for Class A. External carriers and extra pouches are at the officer's expense; ballistic panels are interchangeable and must actually be in the carrier — a carrier with no panels has no ballistic protection. SWAT and BDU carriers contain larger department-provided panels and are worn externally with SWAT and BDU uniforms. Specialty exceptions are only those listed in this section.
rules: Uniformed field, Class A, and Class B: vest is mandatory.
Plainclothes: vest is mandatory when serving a search or arrest warrant, on any enforcement action, when contacting a criminal suspect, or when a supervisor directs it.
oral: You are in plain clothes helping serve an arrest warrant. Is your vest optional?
points.swat: Warrant service always means a vest, including for detectives and for you in plain clothes. Team uniforms use the larger external SWAT carrier.

points.title: Body-Worn Cameras
points.summary: BWCs are described as a transparency and evidence tool. Uniformed officers shall activate the BWC before exiting the vehicle on any dispatched law-enforcement call; shall activate when involved in any manner in a police pursuit, vehicle follow, or fail-to-yield; and shall activate as soon as practical upon deciding to engage in self-initiated law-enforcement activity. Non-uniformed personnel (e.g., detectives) shall activate during pre-planned enforcement events including residential search warrants, serving an arrest warrant, and when arresting a subject. Exigency may warrant turning off or not activating; that decision must be justified (the standard discusses this). There are limits in places such as restrooms/locker rooms when the officer is not there to arrest or serve a warrant. Recordings may be reviewed as authorized in the standard.
