The section notes bargaining constraints on unilateral changes to mandatory subjects.
rules: Activate before exiting the car on a dispatched call.
Activate for pursuits, vehicle follows, and fail-to-yields, and as soon as practical on self-initiated enforcement.
Detectives/plainclothes: activate for pre-planned warrants and arrests.
oral: When must your BWC be on during a residential search warrant?
May you delay activation because a call is 'tactical'?
points.swat: A high-risk warrant, a barricade response, and a pursuit all independently require activation. If a board asks about cameras on a tactical operation, start with this policy and note that Valley SWAT team SOPs (not in these docs) may add team-specific recording rules.
flags: The full BWC standard is long (retention, review, public-records, discipline). This outline focuses on activation duties that matter for tactical/patrol decision-making. Team SOP recording rules were not in the provided documents.

points.title: Unusual Occurrences Coordination and All Hazard Plan (ICS / Mobilization Phases)
points.summary: Deputy Chief(s) coordinate planning for unusual occurrences. All police personnel receive NIMS training as recommended by rank. In a critical incident, planned ICS-style response applies. The first arriving officer is usually the incident commander; the field supervisor establishes a Command Post and serves as IC until a commander arrives; a deputy chief or the Chief may assume command at any time. An EOC is the predetermined facility for Phase III events (Greater Federal Way Community EOC Plan). Phase I: on-duty personnel only (department-wide resources, but not ordinary CIS/Traffic investigative assist); IC may declare; notify per 12.1.2. Phase II: call-in of off-duty personnel or mutual aid to provide patrol services or bring an incident to closure; IC may declare; notify per 12.1.2; not triggered merely by CIS/Traffic investigative assist, Public Works assist under Ch. 61, or a neighboring-agency K-9 request; requires a Significant Incident notification. Phase III: multiple city departments and/or emergency agencies, EOC activated; may cancel vacations and days off; Chief or designee may initiate EOC activation. In a major catastrophe that compromises callback, personnel ensure their families' safety, then respond to the PD in full uniform if able, and report to the Report Writing area for assignment. Phase I/II assembly is wherever the IC designates; Phase III assembly is Report Writing, or the Federal Way Community Center (876 S 33rd St) if the PD is unusable. Communications default to Valley Communications; fallbacks include the admin radio channel (Records coordinating dispatch if towers work), evolving alternatives such as Wi-Fi-capable cell phones, and amateur radio volunteers listed in the Emergency Resources Manual. In Phase II/III, do not take extra equipment (flashlights, cones, spare radios, etc.) without a designated supervisor's authorization. Issued respirators are used per the Respiratory Protection Program. The IC may temporarily reassign functions and may suspend non-emergency calls and/or request mutual aid. Natural/manmade disaster police functions and initial-response practices follow in this standard. The All Hazards Plan is also described as complying with CALEA 46.1.3–46.1.7 (those CALEA numbers are not written as standalone FWPD section headings here).
rules: First arriving officer is IC until a supervisor/commander takes over; Chief/DC may assume at any time.
Phase I = on duty only; Phase II = off-duty call-in or LE mutual aid (Significant Incident required); Phase III = multi-department / EOC.
Neighbor K-9 or ordinary CIS/Traffic investigative response does not, by itself, make it Phase II.
Catastrophe self-report: family safety first, then PD Report Writing (or Community Center if the PD is down), uniform if able.
thresholds: Phase II requires a Significant Incident notification.
Alternate assembly: Federal Way Community Center, 876 S 33rd St.
oral: What is the difference between Phase I, II, and III?
Who is in command when you, a patrol officer, arrive first at a barricade?
If the PD is unusable after a disaster, where do you report?
points.swat: Almost every barricade, hostage, or active assault will be at least Phase I and often Phase II (SWAT call-out and mutual aid). You need to know who is IC, where the CP goes, and that asking for V-SWAT is a commander-level notification decision under 46.1.10 / 46.1.11, not something a first arriving officer freelances without a supervisor.
flags: 12.1.2 (command notification) is referenced throughout and was not in the provided documents.
CALEA 46.1.3–46.1.7 are cited as being satisfied by the All Hazards Plan but are not reproduced as FWPD text.

points.title: Specialized Equipment Cross-Reference; All-Hazards Training; Crowd-Control Training
points.summary: 46.1.8 simply refers specialized equipment to 46.2.3. 46.1.9: documented annual All Hazards / ICS training for affected personnel, and a documented biennial tabletop or full-scale exercise. 46.1.13: sworn employees receive initial and ongoing crowd-control and management training. There is no 46.1.12 in this document.
rules: Annual documented All Hazards/ICS training; biennial tabletop or full-scale exercise.
Ongoing crowd-control training for sworn employees.
thresholds: All Hazards training: annual. Exercise: biennial.
oral: How often does FWPD exercise its All Hazards Plan?
points.swat: Training currency on ICS and crowd control is a baseline for CDU and for any SWAT support of a civil disturbance.
flags: No Standard 46.1.12 appears (numbering jumps 46.1.11 to 46.1.13).

points.section: 46.1.10 (Civil Disturbance, Mass Arrests, Bombs, Hazmat, Clan Labs)
points.title: Specific Incidents — Civil Disturbance, Mass Arrests, Bombs, Hazmat, Clandestine Labs
points.summary: 46.1.10 also contains the hostage/barricade subsection (separate outline). Civil disturbance is an unlawful assembly that is a breach of the peace, or an assembly with imminent danger of collective violence, property destruction, or other unlawful acts. FWPD will try to work with lawful demonstrators in advance. First officers: evaluate from a safe distance, identify leaders or criminals, notify Valley Com and a supervisor, and shall not try to disperse a crowd without sufficient additional police assistance; designate a staging area. The supervisor responds, assesses, and (among other steps) gives an order to disperse before dispersal tactics (the text references Chapter 9A.84). The patrol commander sets the mobilization phase, takes IC at the CP, and may use containment and dialogue, targeted arrests of leaders/agitators, and less-lethal force to disperse — but only with a clear path of escape, and gas/smoke/other less-lethal only coordinated, controlled, and deployed by officers with specialized training on that device. Mass arrests (more than ten) have detailed practices for arrest, juveniles separated from adults, transportation, temporary detention, evidence, security, identification, defense-counsel access (counsel is a right but is not provided at a temporary site in the manner described), court/prosecutor liaison, food/water/sanitation, and medical staging. Bomb threats: primary officer and supervisor practices, evacuation generally left to the person in charge of the building, search practices when a search is prudent. If a device is located, the Bomb Disposal Unit coordinates disposal; CIS is notified if criminal activity is involved. Hazmat: Fire and their HazMat team have scene management and command authority; police support evacuation, traffic, and perimeter. First arriving officers stay back and evaluate from a safe distance. A patrol supervisor responds to Fire's CP. Clan lab: withdraw quickly but safely, detain persons already located, touch nothing and do not alter the environment, notify the field supervisor and Fire, and establish an inner perimeter to prevent entry.
rules: Do not disperse a crowd without enough officers; a failed withdrawal can escalate the event.
Order to disperse before dispersal tactics.
Less-lethal/gas/smoke for crowd dispersal: clear escape path; only specially trained officers deploy the device, under IC coordination.
Mass arrest threshold in this standard: more than ten arrests.
Hazmat: Fire has scene command; police stay back, then support perimeter/evacuation/traffic.
Clan lab: get out, don't touch, notify supervisor and Fire, contain.
thresholds: Mass arrests: more than ten.
Clan lab / hazmat: do not enter to 'see if it is really a lab' once you recognize it.
oral: You are first on a rapidly growing unlawful crowd. What do you not do?
Who has command at a hazmat scene?
You open a door and see a working meth lab. What are your immediate actions?
points.swat: CDU, Bomb Disposal, and SWAT are the regional specialty units listed in 46.2. Crowd-gas in this section does not reprint RCW 10.116.030's four steps or the 'highest elected official' requirement for tear gas at an outdoor riot. You must still follow the statute (see flags).
flags: RCW 10.116.030 is stricter and more specific than the civil-disturbance 'gas/smoke' sentence in 46.1.10. Tear gas (CN, CS, or similar; not OC) may be used only if necessary to alleviate a present risk of serious harm from a riot, barricaded subject, or hostage situation, and only after: (a) exhausting available appropriate alternatives, (b) supervisor authorization based on those circumstances, (c) announcement of intent to use tear gas, and (d) sufficient time and space to comply. For a riot outside a jail/detention facility, authorization from the jurisdiction's highest elected official (in cities, the mayor) is also required. 46.1.10 does not mention those steps. Follow the statute plus policy.
Statutory 'barricaded subject' and 'hostage situation' definitions in RCW 10.116.030(4) differ from the operational definitions in 46.1.10's hostage/barricade subsection. See that outline.

points.title: Hostage / Barricaded Person Situations
points.summary: Philosophy: lives of hostages, civilians, and officers are of the utmost importance; a peaceful resolution will be sought whenever reasonably possible. These practices apply in all hostage and/or barricaded subject situations. FWPD definitions: a Hostage Situation is any situation where an individual is being held by another against his/her will by force or threat of force, expressed or implied. A Barricaded Subject Situation is a criminal suspect or emotionally disturbed person within a definable space, armed with a weapon or with direct access to a deadly weapon, who is not complying with police communication. Patrol officers immediately notify the field supervisor and shall not enter the space controlled by the suspect/subject except when necessary to protect the lives and safety of people other than the suspect/subject, consistent with 'Standard 1.3 Use of Force' (stale cross-reference; use-of-force is now Chapter 4). Inner perimeter as soon as possible; inner-perimeter posts in two-officer contact/cover teams as staffing allows. Outer perimeter as staffing allows, to control ingress/egress; bystanders stay outside it. First arriving officer is IC until a higher-ranking officer takes over; the field supervisor responds and assumes command. IC must: assess whether a crime has been committed; set inner and outer perimeters; after the inner perimeter is in place, attempt contact and request peaceful surrender; make no promises other than a safe detention if the subject complies; establish a CP between the inner and outer perimeters, with room for command, specialty teams, liaisons, and many vehicles; determine whether Phase I may be used; notify the on-duty patrol commander or CDO with enough information to decide on Phase II/III; remain IC until relieved by a commander. The commander decides notifications and Phase II/III, then responds and takes IC. Notifications may include: V-SWAT (contact the designated Valley Commander to activate the team if the commander determines SWAT is necessary); CIS (on-call supervisor for warrants and intelligence); PIO (location is situational); surrounding agencies via Valley Com; and medical/fire, typically staged inside the outer perimeter and outside the inner, possibly near the CP. Evacuate residences and businesses within the outer perimeter as soon as reasonably possible; interview evacuees; if evacuation is impossible due to hazards, contact occupants and advise on sheltering. Evacuate injured persons only if it can be done without creating an unreasonable hazard to police. PIO or designee establishes a media area far enough from the CP and the scene to avoid interference, and asks media not to divulge tactical movements or information.
rules: Do not enter the suspect-controlled space except to protect lives other than the suspect's, consistent with Chapter 4.
Inner perimeter first, then try to contact and call for surrender; promise only a safe detention if they comply.
CP sits between inner and outer perimeters.
V-SWAT is activated by the commander through the designated Valley Commander — not by a freelance first-arriving officer.
Medical stages inside the outer / outside the inner, often near the CP.
No media at the CP; no leaking of tactics.
thresholds: FWPD 'barricaded subject' (operational): definable space + armed or direct access to a deadly weapon + not complying with police communication.
oral: You are first arriving at an armed man who will not come out of an apartment. Walk through your first ten actions.
What may you promise a barricaded subject?
Where do you put the CP, medical, and media?
When may patrol enter the apartment before SWAT arrives?
points.swat: This is the core first-arriving SWAT-support playbook and a very likely oral-board scenario. It also defines the handoff: SWAT later replaces inner-perimeter patrol (46.2.1), but the IC remains responsible for the whole operation.
flags: DEFINITION MISMATCH: RCW 10.116.030(4)(a) defines 'barricaded subject' for tear-gas purposes as a person who is the focus of a law-enforcement intervention, has taken a position that does not allow immediate LE access, and is refusing orders to exit — it does not require that the person be armed. FWPD 46.1.10's operational definition does require a weapon or direct access to a deadly weapon, plus non-compliance with communication. RCW 10.116.030(4)(c) defines a 'hostage situation' as a person held against their will by an armed, potentially armed, or otherwise dangerous suspect. FWPD's hostage definition is holding against the will by force or threat of force, expressed or implied, and does not expressly require that the captor be armed. Use the FWPD definitions for the 46.1.10 response protocol (when to treat it as a barricade/hostage and how to set a perimeter). Use the RCW definitions when the question is whether tear gas is legally authorized. Confirm how Valley SWAT trains this distinction.
46.1.10 still cites 'Standard 1.3 Use of Force.' Use of force is now Chapter 4. Treat 1.3 as a stale cross-reference.

points.title: Active Assaults
points.summary: The core function is to protect people from violent predators. An active shooter or similar mass-casualty incident is initially chaotic, with partial and conflicting information. When such a call is dispatched, commissioned personnel respond (Phase I under 46.1.2 and training bulletin 17-002). First priority: stop the killing. First arriving officers enter and move to locate the killer(s) as 'contact team 1,' even if they enter individually. Objective: contain the assailant(s) so they have no access to more people; locate other dangers (IEDs, hidden assailants). Courses of action: arrest compliant suspects; use force that overcomes resistance; isolate and contain non-compliant suspects who are not actively killing (which may initiate hostage/barricade protocols under 46.1.10); summon BDU and mark possible IEDs, leaving them in place; report weapons fire; remain vigilant for secondary attacks. Keep roadway lanes open for later extraction. Plainclothes officers/detectives don visible 'POLICE' markings. Second priority: establish incident command, a staging manager, and a staging location; after contact 1 enters, all other incoming personnel report to staging. Request mutual aid and Fire/medics to staging. Next: connect the wounded with care — treat in place with a cover officer; and/or a Casualty Collection Point with dedicated protection; and/or a Rescue Task Force (police as force protection for aid/medics). A lieutenant arriving after contact 1 enters goes to the CP and becomes IC until relieved by a commander. Other tasks in the order most relevant: search for additional suspects and hidden/wounded victims (inner perimeter + organized search teams); outer perimeter and traffic control; police protection teams for fire, BDU, or other specialists; evacuate and screen uninjured people at a designated safe location; media staging under the IC/PIO; if a school, a parent-student reunification center; officers at local hospitals for victim ID, security, and evidence. The on-duty commander or CDO decides notifications and takes IC: V-SWAT via the designated Valley Commander if appropriate; CIS (and consider VIIT because of scope); PIO / public warning. Public warning tools include social media, CodeRed (PIO or the City Emergency Manager), and other responsible methods such as Public Works signage. Training: annual refresher for supervisors; active-threat reality-based training every other year for all commissioned officers; annual documented command review of the policy and training needs, which may include a survey of regional/national practice.
rules: First priority: stop the killing. First officers go to the threat as contact 1 — they do not wait to build a four-person team if people are being actively killed.
If the suspect stops actively killing and is contained, transition toward barricade/hostage protocols (46.1.10).
Leave suspected IEDs in place for BDU; mark and report them.
Everyone after contact 1 goes to staging unless assigned.
Medical options: treat in place with cover, CCP, and/or rescue task force.
Plainclothes: visible POLICE markings.
Supervisor refresher annually; officer RBT every other year.
thresholds: Supervisor active-assault training: every calendar year.
Officer reality-based active-threat training: every other year.
oral: You are first arriving at a school with active gunfire. Do you wait for a full team?
You find the shooter down, but a second locked classroom will not open and you hear no more shots. What protocol are you now in?
Where do the second and third arriving officers go if contact 1 is already inside?
points.swat: This is the doctrine that will be running if you arrive as patrol or later as V-SWAT. The 'stop the killing vs. transition to barricade' switch is a classic oral-board decision point, and it is written into this policy. VIIT may investigate because of the size and type of the event, not only because of an OIS.
flags: Training bulletin 17-002 is referenced for the Phase I response and was not provided.
46.1.11's 'Other Considerations' numbering has two items labeled '4' (uninjured people and traffic control) in the extract — a numbering typo, not a missing topic.

points.title: Special Operations Activities — Patrol / SWAT Coordination
points.summary: FWPD participates in regional Bomb Disposal, Special Weapons and Tactics (SWAT), and the Civil Disturbance Unit (CDU); the full team or portions may be activated to help patrol resolve critical incidents. Patrol officers are first responders to many incidents that later involve specialty teams; coordination matters. Patrol responsibilities for those incident types are in 46.1.10. When SWAT deploys, SWAT members will be assigned to replace inner-perimeter patrol units as soon as practical. The SWAT Commander reports to the Incident Commander at the CP. The SWAT Commander has full control of the deployment and use of SWAT members at the scene, but the Incident Commander is responsible for the entire operation. The SWAT Commander shall keep the IC informed of SWAT positions, movements, and observations.
rules: SWAT replaces inner-perimeter patrol as soon as practical.
SWAT Commander controls SWAT deployment and use; the IC owns the overall operation.
SWAT Commander works from the CP, under the IC, and keeps the IC informed.
oral: Who is in charge of a barricade once V-SWAT arrives — the patrol commander or the SWAT commander?
What happens to patrol officers on the inner perimeter when SWAT gets there?
points.swat: This is the command-relationship question. A strong oral-board answer is: 'I do not freelance a team plan. The IC has the incident; the SWAT Commander has the team; I keep information flowing.'

points.title: SWAT Selection
points.summary: FWPD selects officers for SWAT using the process in this standard. Practice A refers the reader to Standard 21.3.2 for the selection process. Practice B requires that applicants for the Tactical Team successfully complete: (1) Physical Assessment; (2) Shooting Qualification; (3) prior to selection, a review by the Chief of the pre-employment psychological — and the sentence ends there in the provided document, mid-thought. No further tests, passing scores, or phase structure are written in this section.
rules: The MOS itself requires a physical assessment, a shooting qualification, and a Chief's review of the pre-employment psychological before selection.
The detailed selection process is referred to Standard 21.3.2, which is not in the provided documents.
thresholds: Passing scores, event standards, and the four selection phases from the announcement are not in 46.2.2. Use the selection announcement and training materials for those numbers, not this MOS section.
oral: What does FWPD policy itself require you to pass to be selected for the tactical team?
points.swat: This is the only SWAT-selection standard in the provided MOS chapters. It is thinner than the selection announcement you already have. You still need 21.3.2 / 16.2.2 from PowerDMS for the formal process language.
flags: INCOMPLETE TEXT: 46.2.2.B.3 ends mid-sentence: 'Prior to selection, a review by the Chief of the pre-employment psychological' — no object (exam, evaluation, etc.) follows. 46.2.4.B.1 ends the same way for Crisis Communications. Do not invent the missing words.

PROCESS CITATION MISMATCH: 46.2.2 points to Standard 21.3.2. 46.2.4 (Crisis Communications) points to Standard 16.2.2. The existing earlier PowerDMS pull list mentioned 16.2.2 as 'Selection for Specialized Assignment.' Both 16.2.2 and 21.3.2 need to be pulled; do not assume they are the same document.

points.title: Specialized Equipment
points.summary: FWPD maintains specialized equipment for unusual occurrences. It is assigned to SWAT and maintained by the assigned commander or designee. Inspection for operational readiness shall occur at least quarterly.
rules: Specialized unusual-occurrence equipment is assigned to SWAT.
Inspect at least quarterly for operational readiness.
thresholds: Inspection interval: at least quarterly.
oral: How often must SWAT-assigned specialized equipment be inspected?
points.swat: If you are selected, equipment readiness is a team duty, not just an armorer's hobby. The MOS does not list NFDD, chemical munitions, or armored-vehicle SOPs — those remain a gap (team SOPs / PowerDMS).
flags: No inventory or SOP for flash-bangs, gas, or armored vehicles appears in this standard.

points.title: Crisis Communications Unit Selection
points.summary: Officers are selected for the Crisis Communications Unit (negotiators / HNT-type assignment) by a process that refers to Standard 16.2.2. The only specific requirement written here is that, prior to selection, the Chief reviews the pre-employment psychological — and, as with 46.2.2, the sentence is incomplete in the provided document.
rules: Crisis Communications selection process is referred to 16.2.2.
A Chief's review of the pre-employment psychological is required before selection (text incomplete).
oral: How does patrol get negotiators to a barricade, and is that the same process as SWAT selection?
points.swat: You will work with this unit on barricades and hostages. Know that it is a separately selected specialty, and that 46.1.10 wants contact after an inner perimeter is up.
flags: Same mid-sentence cutoff as 46.2.2.B.3. Process is in 16.2.2, not 21.3.2.

points.title: Search and Rescue; VIP Security; Special Events
points.summary: 46.2.5: under RCW 38.52.400, FWPD coordinates SAR inside the city; mobilization phases apply. Specialized SAR is by South King County Fire and Rescue or the King County Search and Rescue Association (King County Sheriff affiliate), or other resources with on-duty supervisor approval. If on-duty efforts are beyond capability, the on-duty supervisor responds, notifies the patrol commander or CDO, calls King County Sheriff's communications to request a SAR mission, and coordinates with the KC SAR coordinator. 46.2.6: if a VIP or dignitary visits or stays in the city, the standard assigns planning responsibility; if actual security is required, the SWAT Commander should be considered for the assignment. 46.2.7: special-event planning for public safety, traffic, and crowd control (parades, races, athletic events, etc.), with reference back to 46.2.6 for VIP-related practice.
rules: City SAR is coordinated by FWPD but specialized teams come through KC channels.
If a VIP actually needs security, consider the SWAT Commander for that assignment.
oral: A visiting dignitary needs actual security in Federal Way. Who should be considered to run that?
points.swat: VIP security is a listed SWAT-adjacent mission. SAR is usually not a tactical-team mission unless it evolves.

points.title: Event Deconfliction
points.summary: Event deconfliction is determining when law-enforcement personnel are conducting operations in the same area at the same time (search warrants, arrest operations, surveillance, fugitive apprehension, etc.). Qualifying events shall be entered into RISSafe (or any later Chief-approved successor), online or by telephone at 800-952-5258, as soon as information is available and before the operation (the standard specifies timing and required fields, including a deconfliction radius). If a conflict is identified, the system or watch-center personnel notify the affected agencies so they can coordinate. Training and access are available through the Western States Information Network (WSIN). The standard also covers target/investigative-information deconfliction (subjects, gangs, and similar) through appropriate resources such as WSIN.
rules: Enter qualifying operations into RISSafe (or the approved successor) before the operation, as soon as the information is available.
Phone option: 800-952-5258.
A 'hit' requires coordination with the other agency, not a race to the door.
thresholds: Deconfliction phone: 800-952-5258.
oral: You are planning a high-risk arrest at a Valley address. What deconfliction step must happen before you go?
points.swat: High-risk warrant service and fugitive operations are exactly the events this is built for. A friendly-fire or competing-warrant problem is a planning failure.
flags: The standard lists categories of qualifying events and required data fields in more detail than this outline. Read 46.2.8 in full before running a deconfliction in real life.

points.title: Tactical Operations: Outside Our Jurisdiction
points.summary: The agency with primary territorial jurisdiction must be notified of all preplanned tactical operations at addresses in their jurisdiction. Courtesy notifications are also expected for other LE activity (surveillance, buy-busts, arrests) outside FWPD's territory. Definitions: an internal command-level officer is a Commander (or Acting Commander), Deputy Chief, or Chief. An external command-level contact is a Commander, or, in agencies whose rank structure includes Sergeant as a first-line rank, a Lieutenant or higher. The agency with primary jurisdiction is the one responsible for routine police services at that address. A preplanned tactical operation is any situation, not including fresh pursuit, in which FWPD officers or detectives deploy with the intent to arrest an offender or serve a search warrant at a known location; it does not include typical/mainstream crimes being investigated exclusively inside Federal Way. If FWPD (including SWAT or any valley or combined unit) will conduct such an operation outside primary jurisdiction, an assigned command-level liaison contacts a command-level officer at the host agency before initiation. Those two determine assistance case by case. The host agency is entitled to notification, input into operational decisions in their jurisdiction, and a chance to share safety information. The agency conducting the operation remains responsible for approving all tactics and operational decisions. At a minimum, coordinate: who (rank and name) is IC; a communications representative from each agency; who handles media; who handles follow-up investigation; who handles traffic/crowd control; which radio channel and who monitors it; and what additional resources are needed.
rules: Preplanned tactical ops outside Federal Way require command-level-to-command-level notification before initiation.
Fresh pursuit is excluded from this 'preplanned' definition.
Host agency: notification, input, and safety information. Operating agency: approval of tactics.
Pre-decide IC, comms, media, follow-up, traffic, radio channel, and extra resources.
oral: V-SWAT is serving a high-risk warrant in another Valley city. Who has to talk to whom before you go, and who approves tactics?
Does a fresh pursuit into the next city require this 46.2.9 process?
points.swat: Valley SWAT is regional by nature. This is the mutual-aid / outside-jurisdiction oral-board question, and it is written clearly.
flags: 46.2.9 is about preplanned operations and courtesy notifications. It does not itself write a complete fresh-pursuit or mutual-aid operations SOP.

points.title: Homeland Security
points.summary: The SIU Lieutenant is the department's homeland-security liaison for receiving and coordinating related information (the standard also mentions a bombing-incident bulletin in this part of the chapter). Officers who obtain information that may assist the FBI should provide it to the SIU Lieutenant; if the information is urgent, contact the FBI directly. The department provides community information to help citizens identify terrorism-related suspicious activity. Hazardous-materials awareness training is addressed; prevention includes high-visibility patrol and proactive enforcement. (Hazmat incident command remains with Fire under 46.1.10.)
rules: Routine terrorism-related intel goes to the SIU Lieutenant; urgent information can go straight to the FBI.
Do not confuse this section with Fire's command authority at a hazmat scene (46.1.10).
oral: You get time-sensitive information about a possible bombing plot. Who can you call immediately?
points.swat: Secondary to barricade/active-assault doctrine, but relevant if a threat is terrorism- or IED-related (BDU + FBI path).

cases.name: Graham v. Connor
cases.holding: Excessive-force claims arising from an arrest, investigatory stop, or other seizure are analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's objective-reasonableness standard, not substantive due process. Reasonableness is judged from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene, not with 20/20 hindsight, and allows for split-second judgments in tense, uncertain, and rapidly evolving situations. The officer's subjective intent or motivation is irrelevant.
factors: Severity of the crime at issue
Whether the suspect poses an immediate threat to the safety of officers or others
Whether the suspect is actively resisting or attempting to evade arrest by flight
cases.swat: Every force articulation in a SWAT report or interview should map to Graham, plus Washington's 'necessary' and reasonable-care requirements in RCW 10.120 and FWPD Ch. 4. FWPD 4.1.2 and 4.4.5 expressly incorporate the Graham factors into 'reasonableness' and 'proportional' force.
cases.quiz: Name the three Graham factors and the vantage point a court must use.
cases.answer: Severity of the crime; immediate threat; active resistance or flight. Judged as a reasonable officer on the scene, without hindsight, allowing for split-second decisions.
cases.verified: Restated from earlier study notes; citation matches the official U.S. Reports.

cases.name: Tennessee v. Garner
cases.holding: Using deadly force to prevent escape is a Fourth Amendment seizure. It may not be used unless it is necessary to prevent the escape and the officer has probable cause to believe the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury to the officer or others. Where feasible, some warning must be given. The Court held a statute unconstitutional as applied to an unarmed, non-dangerous fleeing burglary suspect.
cases.swat: This is the federal fleeing-felon rule on a perimeter or a 'squirter.' FWPD 4.1.3 says that if Garner, RCW 9A.16.040, and RCW 10.120.020(2) conflict, defer to 10.120.020(2) (immediate threat: ability, opportunity, intent).
cases.quiz: When may deadly force be used against a fleeing suspect under Garner? What about a warning?
cases.answer: Only if necessary to prevent escape and there is probable cause the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious injury to officers or others. Give a warning where feasible.
cases.verified: Restated from earlier study notes; citation matches the official U.S. Reports.

cases.name: Barnes v. Felix
cases.holding: The Court rejected the Fifth Circuit's 'moment-of-threat' rule, which looked only at the instant the officer was in danger. Excessive-force claims receive a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis that has no time limit: earlier events, including the reasons for the stop and prior interactions, can bear on whether the force was reasonable. The Court expressly did not decide whether or how an officer's own creation of the danger factors in.
cases.swat: Planning, approach, breach, and call-out are on the table, not just the trigger press. That aligns with RCW 10.120.010(8) and FWPD 4.1.2(31): totality includes the officer's own actions. Sound tactics are legal as well as operational.
cases.quiz: What did Barnes reject, and what question did it leave open?
cases.answer: It rejected the moment-of-threat doctrine and held that totality has no time limit. It left open how officer-created danger factors into reasonableness.
cases.verified: Restated from earlier study notes (unanimous opinion of May 15, 2025).

cases.name: Scott v. Harris
cases.holding: An officer's attempt to end a dangerous high-speed chase that threatens innocent bystanders does not violate the Fourth Amendment, even when it puts the fleeing motorist at risk of serious injury or death. Where video blatantly contradicts the plaintiff's version, courts view the facts as shown in the video. There is no magical on/off switch for deadly force; reasonableness is fact-bound.
cases.swat: Federal law is more permissive than Washington and FWPD rules. RCW 10.116.060 and FWPD 41.2.2 / 4.1.5 / 4.4.18 control your pursuit and shooting-at-vehicles decisions. In an interview, show that you know the state and agency rules are stricter.
cases.quiz: Would Scott v. Harris alone justify a pursuit, or shooting at a fleeing car, in Federal Way?
cases.answer: No. FWPD 41.2.2 limits pursuits to felony or DUI (plus the RCW 10.116.060 necessity/risk/supervisor conditions), and 4.1.5 / 4.4.18 tightly limit firing at moving vehicles.

cases.name: Plumhoff v. Rickard
cases.holding: Applying Scott and Graham, the Court held that officers did not violate the Fourth Amendment by using deadly force to end a dangerously reckless high-speed flight that threatened public safety. A temporary near-standstill did not end the threat when the driver immediately tried to resume flight. If deadly force is justified to end a severe public-safety threat, officers need not stop shooting until the threat has ended; firing 15 shots in a roughly 10-second span was not unreasonable on those facts because the driver never abandoned the attempt to flee. The officers were also entitled to qualified immunity.
cases.swat: Cited in earlier study notes as a Barnes-related vehicle-flight case. Useful to show you know the federal rule and immediately contrast it with RCW 10.116.060(3) and FWPD 4.1.5 / 4.4.18: you may not fire on a moving vehicle unless necessary to protect against an imminent threat of serious physical harm from the operator's or a passenger's use of a deadly weapon, and a vehicle is not a deadly weapon unless used as one and no other reasonable means to avoid serious harm are immediately available. Also contrast 'keep shooting until the threat ends' with FWPD 4.4.18: each discharge must be justified.
cases.quiz: Under Plumhoff, may officers continue firing until a fleeing driver's threat has ended? Does that answer control in Federal Way?
cases.answer: Federally, yes, on Plumhoff's facts, if deadly force remains justified. In Federal Way you still must meet RCW 10.116.060(3) and MOS 4.1.5 / 4.4.18, and each shot must be justified. Do not treat Plumhoff as authorization to shoot at a car to end a chase.
cases.verified: Verified 2026-11-24 against the U.S. Reports / official syllabus.

cases.name: County of Los Angeles v. Mendez
cases.holding: The Fourth Amendment does not include the Ninth Circuit's 'provocation rule.' An otherwise reasonable use of force is not rendered unreasonable merely because officers previously committed a separate Fourth Amendment violation that provoked the confrontation. Excessive force is analyzed under Graham's totality test; other constitutional claims (for example, a warrantless entry) are analyzed separately. Plaintiffs may still recover damages proximately caused by the separate violation.
cases.swat: A bad entry does not automatically make a later justified shot an 'excessive force' case under the Fourth Amendment, but the entry can still be its own violation, and Barnes plus Washington's totality definition still put your tactics in the analysis. Do not read Mendez as forgiveness for a sloppy warrant or a Steagald mistake. Plan the entry so you are not creating the emergency.
cases.quiz: What did Mendez reject, and what can a plaintiff still sue over?
cases.answer: It rejected the provocation rule (using an earlier Fourth Amendment violation to convert later reasonable force into excessive force). The plaintiff can still pursue the separate claim (e.g., the unlawful entry) for damages proximately caused by that violation.
cases.verified: Verified 2026-11-24 against the official Supreme Court opinion (No. 16-369, decided May 30, 2017).

cases.name: Payton v. New York (+ Steagald v. United States)
cases.holding: Payton: the Fourth Amendment bars a warrantless, nonconsensual entry into a suspect's home to make a routine felony arrest, absent exigent circumstances. An arrest warrant founded on probable cause carries limited authority to enter the suspect's own dwelling when there is reason to believe the suspect is inside. Steagald: to search a third party's home for the subject of an arrest warrant, you need a search warrant, unless there is consent or exigency.
cases.swat: This is the legal basis for high-risk warrant service. Confirm whose residence it is and the basis for believing the subject is inside. A third-party address means a search warrant.
cases.quiz: A felony arrest-warrant subject is believed to be at his girlfriend's apartment. What do you need to enter?
cases.answer: A search warrant for her apartment (Steagald), unless there is valid consent or exigency.

cases.name: Brigham City v. Stuart + Washington emergency aid (State v. Schultz; State v. Boisselle)
cases.cite: Brigham City, 547 U.S. 398 (2006); Schultz, 170 Wn.2d 746 (2011); Boisselle, 194 Wn.2d 1 (2019)
cases.holding: Brigham City: police may enter a home without a warrant when they have an objectively reasonable basis to believe an occupant is seriously injured or imminently threatened with serious injury; under the Fourth Amendment the officer's subjective motive does not matter. Washington, article I, section 7 is stricter. Schultz applied the emergency-aid exception and reaffirmed that it cannot be a pretext. Boisselle restated a test requiring (1) a subjective belief that an emergency required immediate assistance to protect life or property or prevent serious injury, (2) that a reasonable person would believe the same, and additional limits including that the encounter not be a pretext for a criminal investigation and that there be a nexus to the place entered.
cases.swat: WA is stricter than the federal rule because subjective belief and the absence of pretext both matter. A hasty 'rescue' entry on a warrant or a welfare-check-turned-entry has to be articulated as genuine aid.
cases.quiz: What does Washington require for emergency aid that Brigham City does not?
cases.answer: A subjective belief in a present emergency and no pretext for a criminal investigation (Boisselle/Schultz), on top of objective reasonableness and a nexus to the place.

cases.name: Kentucky v. King
cases.holding: The exigent-circumstances rule applies when police do not create the exigency by engaging or threatening to engage in conduct that violates the Fourth Amendment. If officers lawfully knock and announce and occupants then begin destroying evidence, a warrantless entry to prevent that destruction can be reasonable.
cases.swat: Police-created exigency comes up in knock-and-talks and in surround-and-call-outs that escalate. Article I, section 7 is generally more protective than the Fourth Amendment; do not assume King automatically controls in Washington. Ask a DPA or legal advisor how WA courts apply it.
cases.quiz: Under King, when does police conduct defeat a claimed exigency?
cases.answer: When police created the exigency by engaging or threatening to engage in conduct that violates the Fourth Amendment — for example, threatening an unlawful entry.

cases.name: Knock-and-announce: Wilson, Richards, Banks, Hudson, and State v. Coyle
cases.cite: Wilson v. Arkansas, 514 U.S. 927 (1995); Richards v. Wisconsin, 520 U.S. 385 (1997); United States v. Banks, 540 U.S. 31 (2003); Hudson v. Michigan, 547 U.S. 586 (2006); State v. Coyle, 95 Wn.2d 1 (1980)
cases.holding: Wilson: knock-and-announce is part of Fourth Amendment reasonableness, but countervailing interests can justify an unannounced entry. Richards: no blanket exception for felony drug cases; a no-knock requires reasonable suspicion that knocking would be dangerous, futile, or would inhibit the investigation (e.g., destruction of evidence), decided case by case. Banks: waiting 15–20 seconds before forcing entry was reasonable on those facts where cocaine could be destroyed. Hudson: a knock-and-announce violation does not trigger the federal exclusionary rule. Coyle (WA): RCW 10.31.040 requires, before a nonconsensual entry, that officers announce identity, demand admittance, announce purpose, and be refused (explicitly or implicitly). The purposes are reducing violence, preventing property damage, and protecting privacy.
cases.swat: This is core warrant-service law. Since 2021, RCW 10.31.040(2) bars officers from seeking, and courts from issuing, warrants with an express no-knock exception. Whether an on-scene exigency can still excuse compliance is a case-law / training question — learn how Valley SWAT trains announcement and wait time. Do not rely on Hudson; Washington's remedy and statute are independent.
cases.quiz: List the four Coyle steps before a nonconsensual entry, and the three purposes of the rule. May you seek a no-knock warrant in Washington?
cases.answer: Announce identity, demand admittance, announce purpose, and be refused (explicitly or implicitly). Purposes: reduce violence, prevent property damage, protect privacy. No: RCW 10.31.040(2) bars seeking or issuing a warrant with a no-knock exception.

cases.name: State v. Ladson
cases.holding: Pretextual traffic stops violate article I, section 7 of the Washington Constitution. A traffic stop made as a pretext to conduct an unrelated criminal investigation is a warrantless seizure without the 'authority of law' that a warrant (or a true traffic-code or other valid exception) would provide. Evidence from that stop is suppressed. Article I, section 7 is broader than the Fourth Amendment; Washington is not bound by Whren. Later, State v. Arreola, 176 Wn.2d 284 (2012), permits a mixed-motive stop if a suspected traffic infraction was an actual, conscious, and independent cause of the stop. Ladson itself remains good law on pure pretext.
cases.swat: Less of a 'breach' case than a character-and-search case. It shows you understand that Washington privacy law is stricter than federal law — the same theme as Winterstein, Schultz/Boisselle, and the no-knock statute. Do not use a minor equipment violation as a dishonest way to get to a house or a car you really want to search.
cases.quiz: Does Whren allow a pretextual traffic stop in Washington? What is the Washington rule?
cases.answer: Whren is the federal rule and does not control. Under Ladson, a stop that is merely a pretext for an unrelated investigation violates article I, section 7. A mixed-motive stop may be valid under Arreola if the traffic violation was an actual, conscious, and independent reason for the stop.
cases.verified: Verified 2026-11-24 against the Washington Supreme Court opinion (Justia / CourtListener).
cites: State v. Arreola, 176 Wn.2d 284 (2012) (related later case, flagged as context)

cases.name: State v. Winterstein
cases.holding: Washington does not recognize the inevitable-discovery doctrine under article I, section 7. The Court distinguished inevitable discovery (speculative, and it would admit illegally obtained evidence) from the independent-source doctrine (which Washington does recognize: legally obtained evidence can still support probable cause after tainted information is excluded, and the tainted evidence itself is suppressed). When article I, section 7 is violated, exclusion generally follows to protect privacy and the integrity of the courts.
cases.swat: You cannot fix an unlawful entry or an overbroad search by arguing 'we would have found it anyway when we later got a warrant.' Get the warrant right the first time (Payton/Steagald, knock-and-announce, deconfliction, risk assessment). Independent source is the only close cousin, and it requires a genuinely independent legal path.
cases.quiz: Does Washington recognize inevitable discovery? What about independent source?
cases.answer: No inevitable-discovery doctrine under article I, section 7 (Winterstein). Yes to independent source: legally obtained evidence may still establish probable cause after illegally obtained facts are excluded, but the tainted evidence itself is suppressed.
cases.verified: Verified 2026-11-24 against the Washington Supreme Court opinion.

cases.name: Terry v. Ohio
cases.holding: A police officer may briefly stop a person based on reasonable suspicion — specific, articulable facts, plus rational inferences, that criminal activity may be afoot — which is more than a hunch and less than probable cause. If the officer reasonably believes the person may be armed and presently dangerous, the officer may conduct a narrowly limited pat-down of the outer clothing for weapons. The officer need not be certain the person is armed; the question is whether a reasonably prudent person in those circumstances would be warranted in believing their safety or others' safety was in danger.
cases.swat: Two SWAT-adjacent hooks: (1) RCW 10.120.020(1)(i) / FWPD 4.1.1(1)(i) authorize physical force to prevent or stop flight from a lawful temporary investigative detention only after notice that the person is detained and not free to leave. (2) A weapons frisk is not a general evidence search — important on a perimeter or a detention during a warrant.
cases.quiz: What level of proof is required for a Terry stop, and when may you frisk? When may you use physical force to stop someone fleeing that stop in Washington?
cases.answer: Stop: reasonable suspicion (articulable facts, not a hunch) that crime may be afoot. Frisk: reasonable belief the person may be armed and presently dangerous, limited to a weapons pat-down. Force to stop flight: only if the detention is lawful and the person has been told they are detained and not free to leave (RCW 10.120.020(1)(i); MOS 4.1.1(1)(i)).

cases.name: State v. Arreola
cases.holding: A mixed-motive traffic stop is not pretextual under article I, section 7 if the officer actually, consciously and independently decided that stopping for the suspected traffic infraction was reasonably necessary, even if the officer also hoped to investigate something else. Clarifies Ladson.
cases.swat: Articulate the infraction as an actual, independent reason for the stop in reports and testimony.
cases.quiz: Is a stop pretextual if the officer also wanted to investigate a crime (Arreola)?
cases.answer: Not if a reasonably suspected traffic infraction was an actual, conscious and independent cause of the stop. Pure pretext (Ladson) is still unlawful.

cases.name: State v. Ferrier
cases.verified: Checked 2026-11-26 against the opinion (Justia). Later limited to knock-and-talks to search a home (e.g., State v. Ruem, 2013).
cases.holding: When officers use a knock-and-talk to get consent to search a home, they must first tell the person they may lawfully refuse consent, may revoke it at any time, and may limit its scope. Without those warnings the consent is invalid under article I, section 7.
cases.swat: Knock-and-talk for a home search without a warrant: give all three Ferrier warnings before entry, and document them (body cam).
cases.quiz: What are the Ferrier warnings and when are they required?
cases.answer: Before entering a home on a knock-and-talk to get consent to search: you may refuse consent, you may revoke it at any time, and you may limit the scope.

cases.name: State v. Buelna Valdez
cases.holding: Under article I, section 7, a warrantless vehicle search incident to arrest is allowed only when needed for officer safety or to preserve evidence of the arrest crime that could be concealed or destroyed. Once the arrestee is secured and can't reach the car, the exception doesn't apply; get a warrant or use another exception.
cases.swat: Arrestee cuffed in the back seat = no search incident to arrest of the car in Washington.
cases.quiz: Can you search a car incident to arrest in WA once the arrestee is cuffed in your patrol car?
cases.answer: No (Valdez). The exception exists only for officer safety or preserving evidence the arrestee could reach; get a warrant or another exception.

cases.name: State v. Snapp
cases.holding: Washington does not adopt Gant's 'reasonable to believe evidence of the arrest offense is in the vehicle' branch. Article I, section 7 gives more protection than the Fourth Amendment here.
cases.swat: Federal Gant evidence-branch searches are not lawful in WA state cases.
cases.quiz: Does WA recognize Gant's 'evidence of the offense' branch for vehicle searches (Snapp)?
cases.answer: No. Under article I, section 7 there is no such exception.

cases.name: State v. Z.U.E.
cases.holding: A Terry stop based on a citizen or 911 tip needs indicia of reliability: the informant's reliability or a factual basis for the tip, or officer corroboration of more than innocuous details that suggests criminal activity.
cases.swat: On tip-based stops, document who called, what they saw and how you corroborated the criminal part.
cases.quiz: What does Z.U.E. require before a Terry stop on a tip?
cases.answer: Indicia of reliability (informant reliability or factual basis) or corroboration of more than innocuous facts suggesting criminal activity.

cases.name: State v. Sum
cases.holding: Whether a person is seized under article I, section 7 is judged by whether an objective observer would find that a reasonable person in the same situation would not feel free to leave or decline; that observer is aware that implicit and explicit racial bias has contributed to disproportionate police contacts, and race and ethnicity are part of the totality of the circumstances.
cases.swat: Social contacts can become seizures sooner than you think; be clear when a person is free to go.
cases.quiz: How did Sum change the WA seizure test?
cases.answer: The objective observer considers the person's race and ethnicity and knows bias contributes to disproportionate police contacts.

cases.name: State v. Afana
cases.holding: Washington has no good-faith exception to the exclusionary rule under article I, section 7. Evidence from an unlawful search is suppressed even if the officer acted in good faith.
cases.swat: Officer good faith doesn't save a bad search in state court; get it right up front.
cases.quiz: Does WA recognize a good-faith exception to the exclusionary rule (Afana)?
cases.answer: No.

cases.name: State v. Doughty
cases.holding: Seeing a person make a two-minute, 3:20 a.m. visit to a house suspected of drug activity, without more, is not reasonable suspicion for a Terry stop.
cases.swat: Location and time of night alone aren't enough; articulate specific facts tied to the person.
cases.quiz: Was a short late-night visit to a suspected drug house enough for a stop (Doughty)?
cases.answer: No. Without more specific facts it is not reasonable suspicion.

cases.name: State v. Gunwall
cases.verified: Cited and described in Valdez and other opinions checked 2026-11-26; the Gunwall opinion itself was not separately opened. Flagged.
cases.holding: Sets six nonexclusive factors courts use to decide whether the Washington Constitution gives broader protection than the federal one: text, differences from the federal text, constitutional history, preexisting state law, structural differences, and whether the matter is of particular state or local concern.
cases.swat: Explains why WA search rules are stricter than federal ones (art. I, sec. 7).
cases.quiz: What is Gunwall used for?
cases.answer: Deciding whether the WA Constitution independently gives broader rights than the U.S. Constitution, using six nonexclusive factors.

cases.name: Torres v. Madrid
cases.holding: Using physical force on a person's body with intent to restrain is a Fourth Amendment seizure, even if the person isn't stopped and gets away. (Shooting a fleeing driver who escapes is still a seizure.)
cases.swat: Shots fired at a fleeing suspect who escapes are still a seizure judged under Graham.
cases.quiz: If officers shoot a driver who keeps going and escapes, was there a seizure (Torres)?
cases.answer: Yes. Physical force applied with intent to restrain is a seizure even if the person escapes.

cases.name: Lange v. California
cases.holding: Pursuing a fleeing misdemeanor suspect doesn't automatically justify a warrantless home entry. Officers must look at the facts of each case for a real emergency (e.g., imminent harm, destruction of evidence, escape).
cases.swat: Felony flight into a home is still case-by-case under WA law; misdemeanor flight is not an automatic exigency.
cases.quiz: Is hot pursuit of a misdemeanant always enough for warrantless home entry (Lange)?
cases.answer: No. It's case-by-case; there must be an actual exigency.

cases.name: Caniglia v. Strom
cases.holding: The 'community caretaking' rationale from Cady v. Dombrowski (vehicles) does not create a separate exception allowing warrantless searches and seizures in the home. Emergency aid and exigency rules still apply.
cases.swat: Welfare-check entries must fit emergency aid (Brigham City / Boisselle), not 'caretaking.'
cases.quiz: Is there a community-caretaking exception for entering homes (Caniglia)?
cases.answer: No. Use emergency aid or exigent circumstances analysis instead.

cases.name: Arizona v. Gant
cases.verified: Checked 2026-11-26 against the opinion (Justia, U.S. Reports).
cases.holding: Police may search a vehicle incident to a recent occupant's arrest only if the arrestee is unsecured and within reaching distance of the passenger compartment, or if it is reasonable to believe evidence of the arrest offense might be in the vehicle. (WA rejects the second branch: Snapp; Valdez.)
cases.swat: Federal floor only; Washington is stricter.
cases.quiz: What are Gant's two branches, and which one does WA reject?
cases.answer: (1) Unsecured arrestee within reach; (2) reasonable to believe evidence of the arrest offense is in the vehicle. WA rejects (2) (Snapp).

cases.name: Riley v. California
cases.verified: Checked 2026-11-26 against the opinion (Justia, U.S. Reports).
cases.holding: Police generally need a warrant to search digital data on a cell phone seized during an arrest. Exigent circumstances may still justify a warrantless search in a specific case.
cases.swat: Seize and secure phones; get a warrant to search them.
cases.quiz: Can you search an arrestee's phone data incident to arrest (Riley)?
cases.answer: Generally no; get a warrant (case-specific exigency aside).

rcw.title: Use of force: definitions
rcw.summary: Defines the words that control the statewide force standard: physical force, deadly force, necessary, de-escalation tactics, less lethal alternatives and totality of the circumstances.
points: "Necessary" = no reasonably effective alternative appears to exist AND the force is reasonable and proportional to the lawful purpose or threat.
"Physical force" excludes pat-downs, incidental touching, verbal commands and compliant handcuffing without pain or injury.
"Totality of the circumstances" includes what happened leading up to the force, and the officer's own actions.
De-escalation examples: clear instructions, slowing things down, distance/cover, one officer talking, calling crisis or backup resources.
rcw.quote: the type and amount of physical force or deadly force used is a reasonable and proportional response
text: The definitions in this section apply throughout this chapter unless the context clearly requires otherwise.
(1) "Deadly force" has the same meaning as provided in RCW 9A.16.010.

(2) "De-escalation tactics" refer to actions used by a peace officer that are intended to minimize the likelihood of the need to use force during an incident. Depending on the circumstances, "de-escalation tactics" may include, but are not limited to: Using clear instructions and verbal persuasion; attempting to slow down or stabilize the situation so that more time, options, and resources are available to resolve the incident; creating physical distance by employing tactical repositioning to maintain the benefit of time, distance, and cover; when there are multiple officers, designating one officer to communicate in order to avoid competing commands; requesting and using available support and resources, such as a crisis intervention team, a designated crisis responder or other behavioral health professional, or backup officers.

(3) "Law enforcement agency" includes any "general authority Washington law enforcement agency" and any "limited authority Washington law enforcement agency" as those terms are defined in RCW 10.93.020.
(4) "Less lethal alternatives" include, but are not limited to, verbal warnings, de-escalation tactics, conducted energy weapons, devices that deploy oleoresin capsicum, batons, and beanbag rounds.

(5) "Necessary" means that, under the totality of the circumstances, a reasonably effective alternative to the use of physical force or deadly force does not appear to exist, and the type and amount of physical force or deadly force used is a reasonable and proportional response to effect the legal purpose intended or to protect against the threat posed to the officer or others.

(6) "Peace officer" includes any "general authority Washington peace officer," "limited authority Washington peace officer," and "specially commissioned Washington peace officer" as those terms are defined in RCW 10.93.020; however, "peace officer" does not include any corrections officer or other employee of a jail, correctional, or detention facility, but does include any community corrections officer.

(7) "Physical force" means any act reasonably likely to cause physical pain or injury or any other act exerted upon a person's body to compel, control, constrain, or restrain the person's movement. "Physical force" does not include pat-downs, incidental touching, verbal commands, or compliant handcuffing where there is no physical pain or injury.

(8) "Totality of the circumstances" means all facts known to the peace officer leading up to, and at the time of, the use of force, and includes the actions of the person against whom the peace officer uses such force, and the actions of the peace officer.

rcw.title: Permissible uses of force
rcw.summary: The statewide standard. Physical force only to the extent necessary for listed purposes (arrest, prevent escape, protect against a crime with probable cause, search warrant, stop flight from a lawful detention after notice, imminent threat of bodily injury, etc.). Deadly force only when necessary to protect against an immediate threat of serious physical injury or death. Officers must use reasonable care: de-escalate when possible, least force necessary, stop when necessity ends, less lethal before deadly when possible.
points: Deadly force: "immediate threat" = objectively reasonable belief the person has present and apparent ability, opportunity and intent to immediately cause death or serious bodily injury.

Reasonable care duties (3)(a)–(e): de-escalate when possible; least force necessary; consider characteristics (pregnancy, minor, vulnerable adult, impairment, suicidal, limited English, children present); stop when necessity ends; less lethal before deadly when possible; keep issued less lethal tools available.
Force to stop someone fleeing a Terry detention is allowed only after they've been told they're detained and not free to leave.
Tactics banned by policy or law may be used only to protect a life from an imminent threat.
Agencies may adopt stricter rules (5)(d).
rcw.quote: only when necessary to protect against an immediate threat of serious physical injury or death to the officer or another person
text: (1) PHYSICAL FORCE. Except as otherwise provided under this section, a peace officer may use physical force against a person to the extent necessary to:
(a) Protect against a criminal offense when there is probable cause that the person has committed, is committing, or is about to commit the offense;
(b) Effect an arrest;
(c) Prevent an escape as defined under chapter  9A.76 RCW;
(d) Take a person into custody, transport a person for evaluation or treatment, or provide other assistance under chapter  10.77, 71.05, or  71.34 RCW;
(e) Take a minor into protective custody when authorized or directed by statute;
(f) Execute or enforce a court order authorizing or directing a peace officer to take a person into custody;
(g) Execute a search warrant;

(h) Execute or enforce an oral directive issued by a judicial officer in the courtroom or a written order where the court expressly authorizes a peace officer to use physical force to execute or enforce the directive or order; or

(i) Prevent a person from fleeing or stop a person who is actively fleeing a lawful temporary investigative detention, provided that the person has been given notice that he or she is being detained and is not free to leave;
(j) Take a person into custody when authorized or directed by statute; or
(k) Protect against an imminent threat of bodily injury to the peace officer, another person, or the person against whom force is being used.

(2) DEADLY FORCE. Except as otherwise provided under this section, a peace officer may use deadly force against another person only when necessary to protect against an immediate threat of serious physical injury or death to the officer or another person. For purposes of this subsection: "Immediate threat of serious physical injury or death" means that, based on the totality of the circumstances, it is objectively reasonable to believe that a person has the present and apparent ability, opportunity, and intent to immediately cause death or serious bodily injury to the peace officer or another person.

(3) REASONABLE CARE. A peace officer shall use reasonable care when determining whether to use physical force or deadly force and when using any physical force or deadly force against another person. To that end, a peace officer shall:
(a) When possible, use all de-escalation tactics that are available and appropriate under the circumstances before using physical force;

(b) When using physical force, use the least amount of physical force necessary to overcome resistance under the circumstances. This includes a consideration of the characteristics and conditions of a person for the purposes of determining whether to use force against that person and, if force is necessary, determining the appropriate and least amount of force possible to effect a lawful purpose. Such characteristics and conditions may include, for example, whether the person: Is visibly pregnant, or states that they are pregnant; is known to be a minor, objectively appears to be a minor, or states that they are a minor; is known to be a vulnerable adult, or objectively appears to be a vulnerable adult as defined in RCW 74.34.020; displays signs of mental, behavioral, or physical impairments or disabilities; is experiencing perceptual or cognitive impairments typically related to the use of alcohol, narcotics, hallucinogens, or other drugs; is suicidal; has limited English proficiency; or is in the presence of children;
(c) Terminate the use of physical force as soon as the necessity for such force ends;
(d) When possible, use less lethal alternatives that are available and appropriate under the circumstances before using deadly force; and
(e) Make less lethal alternatives issued to the officer reasonably available for his or her use.

(4) A peace officer may not use any force tactics prohibited by applicable departmental policy, this chapter, or otherwise by law, except to protect his or her life or the life of another person from an imminent threat.
(5) Nothing in this section:

(a) Limits or restricts a peace officer's authority or responsibility to perform lifesaving measures or perform community caretaking functions to ensure health and safety including, but not limited to, rendering medical assistance, performing welfare checks, or assisting other first responders and medical professionals;

(b) Prevents a peace officer from responding to requests for assistance or service from first responders, medical professionals, behavioral health professionals, social service providers, designated crisis responders, shelter or housing providers, or any member of the public;
(c) Permits a peace officer to use physical force or deadly force in a manner or under such circumstances that would violate the United States Constitution or state Constitution; or

(d) Prevents a law enforcement agency or political subdivision of this state from adopting policies or standards with additional requirements for de-escalation and greater restrictions on the use of physical and deadly force than provided in this section.

rcw.title: AG model use-of-force and de-escalation policies
rcw.summary: The Attorney General publishes model use-of-force and de-escalation policies. Every agency must adopt consistent policies or explain its departures to the AG, and must send the AG any later changes within 60 days.
points: Model policies were due July 1, 2022; agency adoption or explanation by Dec 1, 2022.
Policy changes must be sent to the AG within 60 days.
The AG publishes a yearly status report.
rcw.quote: the attorney general shall develop and publish model policies on law enforcement's use of force and de-escalation tactics
text: (1) By July 1, 2022, the attorney general shall develop and publish model policies on law enforcement's use of force and de-escalation tactics consistent with RCW 10.120.020.

(2) By December 1, 2022, all law enforcement agencies shall: Adopt policies consistent with the model policies and submit copies of the applicable policies to the attorney general; or, if the agency did not adopt policies consistent with the model policies, provide notice to the attorney general stating the reasons for any departures from the model policies and an explanation of how the agency's policies are consistent with RCW 10.120.020, including a copy of the agency's relevant policies. After December 1, 2022, whenever a law enforcement agency modifies or repeals any policies pertaining to the use of force or de-escalation tactics, the agency shall submit notice of such action with copies of any relevant policies to the attorney general within 60 days.

(3) By December 31st of each year, the attorney general shall publish on its website a report on the requirements of this section, including copies of the model policies, information as to the status of individual agencies' policies, and copies of any agency policies departing from the model policies.

rcw.title: Chokehold or neck restraint prohibited
rcw.summary: Peace officers may not use a chokehold or any neck restraint (including vascular neck restraints). Agency policies must match.
points: Chokehold = intentional direct pressure on the trachea/windpipe to restrict the airway.
Neck restraint = any vascular neck restraint or hold that presses the neck to constrict blood flow.
Only exception path is RCW 10.120.020(4): a banned tactic to protect a life from an imminent threat.
rcw.quote: A peace officer may not use a chokehold or neck restraint on another person in the course of his or her duties as a peace officer.
text: (1) A peace officer may not use a chokehold or neck restraint on another person in the course of his or her duties as a peace officer.
(2) Any policies pertaining to the use of force adopted by law enforcement agencies must be consistent with this section.
(3) For the purposes of this section:
(a) "Chokehold" means the intentional application of direct pressure to a person's trachea or windpipe for the purpose of restricting another person's airway.
(b) "Neck restraint" refers to any vascular neck restraint or similar restraint, hold, or other tactic in which pressure is applied to the neck for the purpose of constricting blood flow.

rcw.title: Hog-tying prohibited
rcw.summary: Officers may not hog-tie anyone or help put someone in a hog-tie (bound ankles fastened to bound wrists). Doing so counts as excessive force for the duty to intervene. Transport/waist chains and devices that don't fasten ankles to wrists are not covered.
points: Hog-tying = excessive force under RCW 10.93.190, so witnessing officers must intervene and report.
rcw.quote: Hog-tying shall constitute the use of excessive force for the purposes of RCW 10.93.190.
text: (1) A peace officer is prohibited from:
(a) Hog-tying a person; or
(b) Assisting in putting a person into a hog-tie.
(2) Hog-tying shall constitute the use of excessive force for the purposes of RCW 10.93.190.

(3) This section shall not be interpreted to prohibit the use of any other alternative restraint product or device that is administered to reduce the incidence of respiratory fatigue or positional asphyxia if such restraint product or device does not violate this section.
(4) For purposes of this section, "hog-tie" or "hog-tying" means fastening together bound or restrained ankles to bound or restrained wrists. "Hog-tie" or "hog-tying" does not include the following:
(a) Use of transport chains or waist chains to transport prisoners; or
(b) Use of a product or device that does not require bound or restrained ankles to be fastened together to bound or restrained wrists.

rcw.title: Use of tear gas
rcw.summary: Tear gas (CN, CS and similar airborne irritants, not OC) only when necessary to alleviate a present risk of serious harm from a riot, a barricaded subject or a hostage situation. Before using it: exhaust available alternatives, get supervisor authorization, announce, and allow time and space to comply. A riot outside a jail also needs the highest elected official (in a city, the mayor).
points: Barricaded subject = focus of a police effort, in a place without immediate access, refusing orders to exit.
Hostage situation = person held against their will by an armed, potentially armed or otherwise dangerous suspect.
OC is excluded from the definition of tear gas.
rcw.quote: unless necessary to alleviate a present risk of serious harm posed by a: (a) Riot; (b) barricaded subject; or (c) hostage situation.
text: (1) A law enforcement agency may not use or authorize its peace officers or other employees to use tear gas unless necessary to alleviate a present risk of serious harm posed by a: (a) Riot; (b) barricaded subject; or (c) hostage situation.
(2) Prior to using tear gas as authorized under subsection (1) of this section, the officer or employee shall:
(a) Exhaust alternatives to the use of tear gas that are available and appropriate under the circumstances;

(b) Obtain authorization to use tear gas from a supervising officer, who must determine whether the present circumstances warrant the use of tear gas and whether available and appropriate alternatives have been exhausted as provided under this section;
(c) Announce to the subject or subjects the intent to use tear gas; and
(d) Allow sufficient time and space for the subject or subjects to comply with the officer's or employee's directives.

(3) In the case of a riot outside of a correctional, jail, or detention facility, the officer or employee may use tear gas only after: (a) Receiving authorization from the highest elected official of the jurisdiction in which the tear gas is to be used, and (b) meeting the requirements of subsection (2) of this section.
(4) For the purposes of this section:

(a) "Barricaded subject" means an individual who is the focus of a law enforcement intervention effort, has taken a position in a physical location that does not allow immediate law enforcement access, and is refusing law enforcement orders to exit.

(b) "Highest elected official" means the county executive in those charter counties with an elective office of county executive, however designated, and in the case of other counties, the county sheriff. In the case of cities and towns, it means the mayor, regardless of whether the mayor is directly elected, selected by the council or legislative body pursuant to RCW 35.18.190 or  35A.13.030, or selected according to a process in an established city charter. In the case of actions by the Washington state patrol, it means the governor.
(c) "Hostage situation" means a scenario in which a person is being held against his or her will by an armed, potentially armed, or otherwise dangerous suspect.

(d) "Tear gas" means chloroacetophenone (CN), O-chlorobenzylidene malononitrile (CS), and any similar chemical irritant dispersed in the air for the purpose of producing temporary physical discomfort or permanent injury, except "tear gas" does not include oleoresin capsicum (OC).

rcw.title: Military equipment
rcw.summary: Agencies may not acquire or use listed military equipment (e.g., .50 cal+ rifles, machine guns, armed vehicles/drones, explosive or incendiary grenades, LRADs, bayonets). Non-explosive stun, sting, smoke and tear-gas grenades and blast balls are not "grenades" under this section.
points: Less-lethal launchers are not "rifles" under this section.
Federal surplus programs are still allowed for non-military items (medical, protective gear, unarmed vehicles, CEWs).
rcw.quote: "Grenade" does not include other nonexplosive grenades designed to temporarily incapacitate or disorient subjects without causing permanent injury
text: (1) A law enforcement agency may not acquire or use any military equipment. Any law enforcement agency in possession of military equipment as of July 25, 2021, shall return the equipment to the federal agency from which it was acquired, if applicable, or destroy the equipment by December 31, 2022.

(2)(a) Each law enforcement agency shall compile an inventory of military equipment possessed by the agency, including the proposed use of the equipment, estimated number of times the equipment has been used in the prior year, and whether such use is necessary for the operation and safety of the agency or some other public safety purpose. The agency shall provide the inventory to the Washington association of sheriffs and police chiefs no later than November 1, 2021.

(b) The Washington association of sheriffs and police chiefs shall summarize the inventory information from each law enforcement agency and provide a report to the governor and the appropriate committees of the legislature no later than December 31, 2021.
(3) For the purposes of this section:

(a) "Military equipment" means rifles of .50 caliber or greater, machine guns, armed helicopters, armed or armored drones, armed vessels, armed vehicles, armed aircraft, tanks, long range acoustic hailing devices, rockets, rocket launchers, bayonets, grenades, missiles, directed energy systems, and electromagnetic spectrum weapons.

(b) "Grenade" refers to any explosive grenade designed to injure or kill subjects, such as a fragmentation grenade or antitank grenade, or any incendiary grenade designed to produce intense heat or fire. "Grenade" does not include other nonexplosive grenades designed to temporarily incapacitate or disorient subjects without causing permanent injury, such as a stun grenade, sting grenade, smoke grenade, tear gas grenade, or blast ball.

(c) "Rifle" has the same meaning as provided under RCW 9.41.010, except "rifle" does not include: Any shotgun, as defined under RCW 9.41.010; any device designed or used to deploy less lethal munitions including, but not limited to, rubber, bean bag, soft nose, sponge, or other nonpenetrating impact rounds; or any less lethal equipment.

(4) This section does not prohibit a law enforcement agency from participating in a federal military equipment surplus program, provided that any equipment acquired through the program does not constitute military equipment. This may include, for example: Medical supplies; hospital and health care equipment; office supplies, furniture, and equipment; school supplies; warehousing equipment; unarmed vehicles and vessels; conducted energy weapons; public address systems; scientific equipment; and protective gear and weather gear.

rcw.title: Officers reasonably identifiable
rcw.summary: Agencies must make sure uniformed on-duty officers are reasonably identifiable: the uniform shows the officer's name or other information the public can see and the agency can use to identify the officer.
rcw.quote: the peace officer's uniform clearly displays the officer's name or other information that members of the public can see
text: All law enforcement agencies shall adopt policies and procedures to ensure that uniformed peace officers while on duty and in the performance of their official duties are reasonably identifiable. For purposes of this section, "reasonably identifiable" means that the peace officer's uniform clearly displays the officer's name or other information that members of the public can see and the agency can use to identify the peace officer.

rcw.title: Vehicular pursuit; shooting at moving vehicles
