cards.a: At least annually for firearms and ECWs (and annual in-service on UOF policies). Non-lethal weapons and weaponless control techniques: at least biennially under 4.3.3. Defensive-tactics training is also annual under 4.4.21.

cards.q: How many qualification attempts are allowed in a single day?
cards.a: No more than five. (MOS 4.3.3.C.)

cards.q: What happens if a non-probationary officer fails primary service-pistol qualification?
cards.a: The officer is not entirely disarmed. The work assignment is temporarily modified so they have reduced contact with the public and no contact with suspected violators, and authorization to carry that weapon type is otherwise suspended until proficiency is shown. (MOS 4.3.2, 4.3.3.)

cards.q: Define 'necessary' as used in MOS 4.4.5.
cards.a: A reasonably effective alternative does not appear to exist, and the use of force must be a reasonable and proportional response.

cards.q: When safe and feasible, what four things shall officers do before using physical force (MOS 4.4.7)?
cards.a: Identify themselves as police officers; attempt to determine whether the person has a condition that may affect ability to understand and comply; provide clear instructions and warnings, including that physical force will be used unless resistance ceases; and give a reasonable opportunity to comply.

cards.q: May you use deadly force against a person who is a danger only to themselves?
cards.a: No. MOS 4.4.15 and 4.4.18 prohibit deadly force, and prohibit discharging or pointing a firearm, at a person who presents a danger only to themselves and does not have the apparent ability, opportunity, and intent to immediately cause death or serious bodily injury to the officer or another person.

cards.q: Besides shooting, what else does MOS 4.4.15 list as deadly force?
cards.a: Intentional impact-weapon strikes to the head, neck, throat, or spine; intentionally striking a person's head into a hard, fixed object; discharging a firearm loaded with lethal ammunition at a person; and intentionally striking with a vehicle a person who is not inside a vehicle.

cards.q: What less-lethal tools does MOS 4.4.16 list?
cards.a: Taser (ECW), OC spray, ASP or wooden baton, 40mm launcher, FN 303, and personal impact weapons (hands, feet, elbows, knees).

cards.q: What is the standard ECW cycle, and what should you do after three cycles if the person continues to aggress?
cards.a: One standard discharge cycle of five seconds or less, then reassess. Use only the minimum number of cycles necessary. After three applications, assume the ECW may not be effective and consider other options. Articulate each application. (MOS 4.4.17.)

cards.q: When should you not use an ECW (list at least four MOS 4.4.17 limits)?
cards.a: On a fleeing person, absent other factors; on a handcuffed or otherwise restrained person unless deadly force is authorized (see also the narrower 4.1.9 contact-stun/escape rules); on a person on an elevated surface unless fall injury has been reasonably mitigated; on an operator in physical control of a vehicle in motion unless deadly force is authorized; in a flammable, volatile, or explosive environment; and generally not targeting head, neck, chest, or genitals.

cards.q: May you use a closed-fist or knee strike to the head as pain compliance?
cards.a: No. Striking techniques directed at the head may be used only as self-defense or defense of others, not as pain compliance. (MOS 4.4.14.) Intentional impact-weapon strikes to the head/neck/throat/spine are deadly force (4.4.15, 4.4.17).

cards.q: Name at least four asphyxia-prevention rules in MOS 4.4.11.
cards.a: Roll the person to the side and to an upright position that does not impede breathing, except if unconscious; do not put prolonged pressure on the chest, neck, or back (including sitting, kneeling, or standing); continuously monitor breathing, color, and verbalized impairment; designate a Safety Officer when possible; do not transport a person in the prone position.

cards.q: May you hog-tie a person or leave them face-down in a hobble?
cards.a: No. Do not connect a hobble to rear handcuffs. Once a hobble is applied, do not place the person face down. Monitor them and discontinue the hobble when necessity ends. Agency-issued hobbles only. (MOS 4.4.20.)

cards.q: A subject vomits while wearing a spit guard. What do you do?
cards.a: Promptly remove and discard the spit guard. Spit guards also shall not be applied if the person is bleeding profusely around the mouth or nose, or has a medical condition affecting breathing or shows labored or distressed breathing. After application, move to a seated or side-recovery position and monitor. (MOS 4.4.19.)

cards.q: Must each firearm discharge be separately justified? Must you warn before shooting when feasible?
cards.a: Yes and yes. Officers are only permitted to discharge a firearm at a person when deadly force is authorized; each discharge must be justified; and when feasible, officers shall give a verbal warning that a firearm will be discharged. (MOS 4.4.18.)

cards.q: What are FWPD patrol minimum staffing levels?
cards.a: Seven officers from midnight to 1400, and nine officers from 1400 to midnight. Traffic and K-9 may count; contract-services positions may not. A lieutenant may operate below minimum for short periods (1–2 hours) during unanticipated shortages. (MOS 41.1.1.)

cards.q: When is a priority (lights-and-siren) response authorized under MOS 41.2.1?
cards.a: Officer needs assistance (Code 2 or Code 3); calls involving seriously injured persons or an imminent threat to life or serious bodily injury; collisions with a probable report of a seriously injured person; felony crimes in progress; or when authorized by a supervisor. The officer remains responsible for safe operation and may drop to routine for safety or for a stealthy last approach.

cards.q: What is a 'vehicular pursuit' under RCW 10.116.060(5) / MOS 41.2.2?
cards.a: An attempt by a uniformed peace officer in a vehicle equipped with emergency lights and a siren to stop a moving vehicle, where the operator appears aware of the stop signal and appears to be willfully resisting or ignoring it by increasing speed, making evasive maneuvers, or driving recklessly in a way that endangers the community or the officer. It is not a pursuit if the violator slows and appears to be looking for a place to stop.

cards.q: Under FWPD policy, for what crimes may you initiate a vehicle pursuit?
cards.a: When you have reasonable suspicion or probable cause that the driver or occupants have committed or are about to commit a felony, or DUI under RCW 46.61.502. The crime of eluding is not sufficient as the sole reason to initiate, authorize, or continue a pursuit. (MOS 41.2.2.B.)

cards.q: How does current RCW 10.116.060 (I-2113) differ from FWPD 41.2.2 on when a pursuit may start?
cards.a: The statute (2024 c 6) allows a pursuit if there is reasonable suspicion the person violated the law, the pursuit is necessary to identify or apprehend, the person poses a threat to the safety of others, and the risks of not apprehending outweigh the risks of the pursuit, plus supervisor and training conditions. FWPD policy is stricter: felony or DUI only, and eluding alone is not enough. Follow the policy; you may always be stricter than the statute.

cards.q: What training and equipment must a pursuit driver have under MOS 41.2.2?
cards.a: EVOC within the last 24 months, including instruction on ongoing risk analysis and mitigation; trained and authorized in at least one pursuit-intervention technique (tire deflation or PIT); wearing a police uniform; driving a police vehicle equipped with emergency lights and siren (and not a banned specialty vehicle).

cards.q: May the SWAT truck, bomb truck, or a unit transporting a prisoner join a pursuit?
cards.a: No. Those vehicles shall not initiate or become involved in a pursuit. (MOS 41.2.2.E.4.)

cards.q: How many police vehicles may normally be in a pursuit?
cards.a: Normally up to three. Additional units may be authorized based on the number of suspects, reason to believe they are armed, the threat to life, or when PIT is authorized. (MOS 41.2.2.F.)

cards.q: When must a pursuit be terminated under MOS 41.2.2?
cards.a: If the primary officer, field supervisor, or patrol commander believes there is unreasonable danger that outweighs the need for apprehension; if the suspect's identity is established and later apprehension can be accomplished without a need for immediate apprehension; if traffic, roadway, or environmental conditions indicate the futility of continued pursuit; or if the pursued vehicle's location is no longer known. Also terminate if statutory or policy requirements are not met (RCW 10.116.060(3)). On termination, turn off emergency equipment and obey the rules of the road.

cards.q: At what speed does PIT require the monitoring supervisor's authorization?
cards.a: At speeds above 40 mph. At 40 mph and under, PIT is available to officers who have completed the prescribed course. Officers will not be disciplined for deciding not to PIT. (MOS 41.2.3.)

cards.q: When may you use boxing-in, tire deflation, ramming, or a roadblock?
cards.a: Boxing-in: supervisor or commander approval, and only if there is no reason to believe the fleeing person is armed with a firearm; no intentional contact. Tire deflation: supervisor authorization, and notify pursuing units of the location. Ramming / forcing off the road, and physical roadblocks: only in circumstances justifying deadly force, and with supervisor or commander approval. (MOS 41.2.3.)

cards.q: May you pursue the wrong way on a freeway or divided highway?
cards.a: No. Officers shall not pursue suspects the wrong way on interstate or other controlled-access highways, or on any divided highway. (MOS 41.2.3.)

cards.q: When must a non-uniformed officer wear a protective vest?
cards.a: When serving a search and/or arrest warrant; when engaging in any enforcement action; when contacting a criminal suspect; or when a commissioned supervisor directs it. Otherwise vest wear is optional when not in uniform. Class A, Class B, and field uniforms require a vest. (MOS 41.3.5.)

cards.q: When must a uniformed officer activate a body-worn camera?
cards.a: Before exiting the vehicle on any dispatched law-enforcement call; when involved in any manner in a police pursuit, vehicle follow, or fail-to-yield; and as soon as practical upon deciding to engage in self-initiated law-enforcement activity. Detectives shall activate during pre-planned enforcement including residential search warrants, arrest-warrant service, and arrests. (MOS 41.3.8.)

cards.q: Who is incident commander when you, a patrol officer, arrive first at a critical incident?
cards.a: In most cases the first arriving officer becomes the IC, until the field supervisor establishes a command post and assumes command, until a commander arrives, or until a deputy chief or the Chief assumes command. (MOS 46.1.2.)

cards.q: Define Mobilization Phases I, II, and III.
cards.a: Phase I: on-duty personnel only (department-wide), declared by the IC; notify per 12.1.2. Phase II: call-in of off-duty personnel or LE mutual aid to provide patrol or close the incident; IC may declare; Significant Incident notification required. Phase III: multiple city departments and/or emergency agencies, EOC activated; Chief or designee may initiate EOC activation; vacations/days off may be canceled. (MOS 46.1.2.)

cards.q: Does requesting a neighboring-agency K-9, or ordinary CIS/Traffic investigative help, automatically create a Phase II mobilization?
cards.a: No. Those are expressly excluded from the Phase II definition. (MOS 46.1.2.)

cards.q: In a major catastrophe, where do you report, and what do you do first?
cards.a: Ensure your family's safety first, then respond to the Police Department in full uniform if able, and report to the Report Writing area for assignment. If the PD is unusable, report to the Federal Way Community Center, 876 S 33rd St. (MOS 46.1.2.)

cards.q: How often is All Hazards / ICS training, and how often is the plan exercised?
cards.a: Documented annual training on the All Hazards Plan and ICS for affected personnel, and a documented biennial tabletop or full-scale exercise. (MOS 46.1.9.)

cards.q: What is FWPD's operational definition of a barricaded subject situation (MOS 46.1.10)?
cards.a: A criminal suspect or emotionally disturbed person is within a definable space, is armed with a weapon or has direct access to a deadly weapon, and is not complying with police communication.

cards.q: What is FWPD's operational definition of a hostage situation (MOS 46.1.10)?
cards.a: Any situation where an individual is being held by another against his or her will by force or threat of force, expressed or implied.

cards.q: How does the RCW 10.116.030 'barricaded subject' definition differ from FWPD 46.1.10?
cards.a: The statute (for tear-gas purposes) requires that the person is the focus of a law-enforcement intervention, has taken a position that does not allow immediate access, and is refusing orders to exit — it does not require that the person be armed. FWPD's operational definition does require a weapon or direct access to a deadly weapon, plus non-compliance with communication. Use the MOS definition for the 46.1.10 response protocol; use the RCW definition when deciding if tear gas is legally authorized.

cards.q: When may first-arriving patrol enter a barricaded subject's space before SWAT arrives?
cards.a: Officers shall not enter the space controlled by the suspect/subject except when necessary to protect the lives and safety of people other than the suspect/subject, consistent with the use-of-force policy (now Chapter 4). (MOS 46.1.10.)

cards.q: After an inner perimeter is up, what may you promise a barricaded subject?
cards.a: Make no promises other than a safe detention if the subject peacefully complies with police instructions. (MOS 46.1.10.)

cards.q: Where should the incident command post, medical, and media be placed at a barricade?
cards.a: CP: between the inner and outer perimeters, with room for command, specialty teams, liaisons, and many vehicles. Medical/fire: typically inside the outer perimeter and outside the inner, possibly near the CP. Media: a gathering area far enough from the CP and the scene to prevent interference; ask media not to divulge tactics. (MOS 46.1.10.)

cards.q: Who activates Valley SWAT for a barricade or active assault?
cards.a: If the commander determines SWAT is necessary or appropriate, he or she contacts the designated Valley Commander to activate the team. (MOS 46.1.10, 46.1.11.)

cards.q: In an active assault, what is the first priority, and do the first officers wait for a full team?
cards.a: First priority: stop the killing. First arriving officers enter and move to locate the killer(s) as contact team 1, even if they enter individually. They do not wait to build a larger team while people are being actively killed. (MOS 46.1.11.)

cards.q: If an active-assault suspect is no longer actively killing but will not comply, what protocol may you transition to?
cards.a: Isolate and contain non-compliant suspects who are not actively killing. This may initiate hostage or barricaded-subject protocols under MOS 46.1.10. (MOS 46.1.11.)

cards.q: What should you do with a suspected IED during an active assault?
cards.a: Leave it in place, mark the location, and summon BDU personnel to handle it. Watch for secondary attacks. (MOS 46.1.11.)

cards.q: Name the three ways MOS 46.1.11 says you may get medical care to the wounded during an active assault.
cards.a: Treat in place (with a cover officer); a Casualty Collection Point with dedicated protection; and/or a Rescue Task Force (police as force protection for aid/medics).

cards.q: Where do officers arriving after contact 1 go in an active assault?
cards.a: To the designated staging location for assignment. A lieutenant arriving after contact 1 enters goes to the command post and becomes IC until relieved by a commander. Plainclothes personnel don visible POLICE markings. (MOS 46.1.11.)

cards.q: How often is active-threat refresher training required?
cards.a: Every calendar year for supervisors. Reality-based active-threat training every other year for all commissioned officers. A commander also reviews the policy and training annually. (MOS 46.1.11.E.)

cards.q: Once V-SWAT arrives at a barricade, who controls the team and who owns the incident?
cards.a: The SWAT Commander has full control over the deployment and use of SWAT members. The Incident Commander is responsible for the entire operation. The SWAT Commander reports to the IC at the CP and keeps the IC informed of positions, movements, and observations. SWAT replaces inner-perimeter patrol as soon as practical. (MOS 46.2.1.)

cards.q: What tests does MOS 46.2.2 say a SWAT applicant must complete?
cards.a: A physical assessment, a shooting qualification, and, prior to selection, a review by the Chief of the pre-employment psychological (the sentence is incomplete in the source). The broader selection process is referred to Standard 21.3.2, which was not in the provided documents.

cards.q: How often must SWAT-assigned specialized equipment be inspected?
cards.a: At least quarterly, to ensure operational readiness. The equipment is assigned to SWAT and maintained by the assigned commander or designee. (MOS 46.2.3.)

cards.q: What deconfliction system does FWPD use, and when must an operation be entered?
cards.a: RISSafe (or a later Chief-approved successor), online or by phone at 800-952-5258. Qualifying events (warrants, arrest operations, surveillance, fugitive apprehension, and other high-risk or special investigations) shall be entered as soon as information is available and before the operation. (MOS 46.2.8.)

cards.q: Before a preplanned FWPD or V-SWAT tactical operation outside Federal Way, what notification is required?
cards.a: An assigned command-level liaison (Commander / Acting Commander, Deputy Chief, or Chief) must contact a command-level officer at the agency with primary jurisdiction before initiating the operation. The host agency gets notification, input, and a chance to share safety information. The operating agency remains responsible for approving tactics. Fresh pursuit is excluded from this 'preplanned' rule. (MOS 46.2.9.)

cards.q: List at least five items the two agencies must coordinate under MOS 46.2.9.
cards.a: Who (rank and name) is Incident Commander; a communications representative from each agency; who handles media; who handles follow-up investigation; who handles traffic/crowd control; which radio channel and who monitors it; and what additional resources are needed.

cards.q: You arrive first at a suspected clan lab. What do you do?
cards.a: Quickly but safely withdraw, detain anyone already located, do not touch anything or alter the environment, immediately notify the field supervisor and the Fire Department, and establish an inner perimeter to prevent entry. (MOS 46.1.10.)

cards.q: Who has scene command at a hazardous-materials incident?
cards.a: The Fire Department and their Hazardous Materials Response Team have scene management and command authority. Police support evacuation, traffic, and perimeter, and first officers stay back and evaluate from a safe distance. (MOS 46.1.10.)

cards.q: What should you not do when first arriving at a civil disturbance?
cards.a: Do not attempt to disperse a crowd without sufficient additional police assistance. A withdrawal after an under-strength dispersal attempt can cause the disturbance to escalate. Evaluate from a safe distance, notify Valley Com and a supervisor, and set a staging area. An order to disperse comes before dispersal tactics. (MOS 46.1.10.)

cards.q: What four steps must precede tear-gas use under RCW 10.116.030(2)?
cards.a: (1) Exhaust alternatives that are available and appropriate; (2) obtain authorization from a supervising officer, who must determine that present circumstances warrant tear gas and that alternatives have been exhausted; (3) announce the intent to use tear gas; (4) allow sufficient time and space to comply. Tear gas may be used only if necessary to alleviate a present risk of serious harm from a riot, barricaded subject, or hostage situation. A riot outside a jail also requires authorization from the highest elected official (in cities, the mayor).

cards.q: If you obtain urgent information that may assist the FBI, may you call the FBI directly?
cards.a: Yes. Routine information goes to the SIU Lieutenant; if the officer deems the information urgent, the officer should contact the FBI directly. (MOS 46.3.2.)

cards.q: Name the three Graham factors and the required vantage point.
cards.a: Severity of the crime; whether the suspect poses an immediate threat to officers or others; whether the suspect is actively resisting or fleeing. Judged from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene, without 20/20 hindsight, allowing for split-second decisions. (Graham v. Connor, 490 U.S. 386 (1989).)

cards.q: When may deadly force be used against a fleeing suspect under Tennessee v. Garner?
cards.a: Only if it is necessary to prevent escape and the officer has probable cause to believe the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury to the officer or others. Give a warning where feasible. (471 U.S. 1 (1985).)

cards.q: What did Barnes v. Felix (605 U.S. 73 (2025)) reject, and what did it leave open?
cards.a: It rejected the 'moment-of-threat' rule (looking only at the instant of danger) and held that totality-of-circumstances analysis has no time limit. It left open how an officer's own creation of danger factors into reasonableness.

cards.q: Would Scott v. Harris or Plumhoff v. Rickard alone authorize shooting at a fleeing car in Federal Way?
cards.a: No. Those cases are more permissive under the Fourth Amendment. In Federal Way you must still meet RCW 10.116.060(3) and MOS 4.1.5 / 4.4.18, and FWPD 41.2.2's felony-or-DUI pursuit limit. Each firearm discharge must be justified.

cards.q: Under Plumhoff v. Rickard, 572 U.S. 765 (2014), what did the Court say about continuing to fire during a dangerous vehicle flight?
cards.a: If deadly force is justified to end a severe public-safety threat, officers need not stop shooting until the threat has ended. On those facts, 15 shots in about 10 seconds were not unreasonable because the driver never abandoned the attempt to flee. This federal holding does not override RCW 10.116.060(3) or MOS 4.1.5 / 4.4.18.

cards.q: What 'provocation rule' did County of Los Angeles v. Mendez, 581 U.S. 420 (2017), reject?
cards.a: The Ninth Circuit rule that an otherwise reasonable use of force could be deemed excessive because officers had earlier committed a separate Fourth Amendment violation that provoked the confrontation. Excessive force is analyzed under Graham; other claims (such as an unlawful entry) are analyzed separately, and damages can still flow from that separate violation.
cards.ref: County of Los Angeles v. Mendez

cards.q: Payton vs. Steagald: what warrant do you need to enter a suspect's own home vs. a third party's home?
cards.a: Suspect's own home: an arrest warrant plus reason to believe the suspect is inside (or consent or exigency). Third party's home: a search warrant (or consent or exigency). (Payton, 445 U.S. 573 (1980); Steagald, 451 U.S. 204 (1981).)

cards.q: What extra showing does Washington require for emergency-aid entry compared with Brigham City?
cards.a: A subjective belief that a present emergency requires immediate aid, and that the entry is not a pretext for a criminal investigation, plus objective reasonableness and a nexus to the place (Schultz; Boisselle). Brigham City is objective only.

cards.q: Under Kentucky v. King, when does police conduct defeat a claimed exigency?
cards.a: When police created the exigency by engaging or threatening to engage in conduct that violates the Fourth Amendment. A lawful knock-and-announce that then leads occupants to start destroying evidence can still support an exigency entry. Confirm how Washington courts apply this under article I, section 7.

cards.q: List the four State v. Coyle steps before a nonconsensual entry, and may you seek a no-knock warrant in Washington?
cards.a: Announce identity, demand admittance, announce purpose, and be refused (explicitly or implicitly). Purposes: reduce violence, prevent property damage, protect privacy. You may not seek, and a court may not issue, a warrant with a no-knock exception (RCW 10.31.040(2)).

cards.q: What did State v. Ladson, 138 Wn.2d 343 (1999), hold about pretextual traffic stops?
cards.a: Pretextual traffic stops violate article I, section 7. A stop used merely as a device to conduct an unrelated investigation is a warrantless seizure without 'authority of law.' Washington is not bound by Whren. (A later case, Arreola, allows a mixed-motive stop if the traffic violation was an actual, conscious, and independent cause.)

cards.q: Does Washington recognize the inevitable-discovery doctrine?
cards.a: No. State v. Winterstein, 167 Wn.2d 620 (2009), rejected inevitable discovery under article I, section 7. Washington does recognize the independent-source doctrine: legally obtained evidence may still support probable cause after tainted facts are excluded, but the illegally obtained evidence itself is suppressed.

cards.q: What does Terry v. Ohio require for a stop and for a frisk?
cards.a: Stop: reasonable suspicion — specific, articulable facts plus rational inferences that crime may be afoot, more than a hunch. Frisk: a reasonable belief the person may be armed and presently dangerous, limited to a pat-down of the outer clothing for weapons. (392 U.S. 1 (1968).)

cards.q: What is Washington's statutory no-knock rule?
cards.a: RCW 10.31.040(2) (2021 c 320 § 8) bars officers from seeking, and courts from issuing, warrants that include an express exception to the knock-and-announce requirement. The knock-and-announce duty in 10.31.040(1) and State v. Coyle still apply.

cards.q: What is the duty to intervene and to report wrongdoing under RCW 10.93.190 / MOS 4.4.9?
cards.a: Any identifiable on-duty officer who witnesses another officer engaging or attempting to engage in excessive force shall intervene when in a position to do so. Any identifiable on-duty officer who witnesses any wrongdoing committed by another officer shall report it to a supervisor. MOS 4.4.9 in this revision does not itself state a 30-second timing rule.

cards.q: What are the three purposes of knock-and-announce under State v. Coyle?
cards.a: Reduce violence, prevent property damage, and protect privacy.

cards.q: Does Hudson v. Michigan mean a knock-and-announce violation has no consequence in Washington?
cards.a: No. Hudson holds only that a knock-and-announce violation does not trigger the federal exclusionary rule. Washington has its own statute (RCW 10.31.040), Coyle, and a generally more protective article I, section 7. Do not rely on Hudson as permission to skip announcement.

cards.q: Under RCW 10.120.010, what two things make force "necessary"?
cards.a: (1) Under the totality of the circumstances, a reasonably effective alternative to force does not appear to exist, and (2) the type and amount of force is a reasonable and proportional response to the lawful purpose or the threat.

cards.q: Does RCW 10.120's "physical force" include compliant handcuffing?
cards.a: No. Pat-downs, incidental touching, verbal commands and compliant handcuffing with no pain or injury are excluded.

cards.q: When may a WA peace officer use deadly force under RCW 10.120.020(2)?
cards.a: Only when necessary to protect against an immediate threat of serious physical injury or death to the officer or another person: an objectively reasonable belief the person has the present and apparent ability, opportunity and intent to immediately cause death or serious bodily injury.

cards.q: List the reasonable-care duties in RCW 10.120.020(3).
cards.a: When possible use available, appropriate de-escalation before physical force; use the least force necessary (considering the person's characteristics and conditions); stop force when necessity ends; when possible use less lethal alternatives before deadly force; keep issued less lethal alternatives reasonably available.

cards.q: Can you use force to stop someone walking away from a Terry stop in WA?
cards.a: Yes, if necessary, but only after the person has been given notice that they are being detained and are not free to leave (RCW 10.120.020(1)(i)).

cards.q: What must an agency do after changing its use-of-force policy (RCW 10.120.030)?
cards.a: Send notice and copies of the relevant policies to the Attorney General within 60 days.

cards.q: Define "neck restraint" under RCW 10.116.020.
cards.a: Any vascular neck restraint or similar restraint, hold or tactic in which pressure is applied to the neck to constrict blood flow. Banned for WA peace officers, along with chokeholds.

cards.q: Is hog-tying allowed in WA? What else follows from it?
cards.a: No (RCW 10.116.022). It is defined as excessive force for the duty to intervene (RCW 10.93.190), so other officers must intervene and report.

cards.q: Four steps before tear gas under RCW 10.116.030(2)?
cards.a: (1) Exhaust available, appropriate alternatives; (2) get authorization from a supervising officer; (3) announce the intent to use tear gas; (4) allow sufficient time and space to comply.

cards.q: Who must authorize tear gas for a riot in Federal Way (outside a jail)?
cards.a: The highest elected official of the jurisdiction (for a city, the mayor), plus the normal 10.116.030(2) steps.

cards.q: Is OC spray "tear gas" under RCW 10.116.030?
cards.a: No. The definition covers CN, CS and similar airborne irritants and expressly excludes oleoresin capsicum (OC).

cards.q: Are stun (flash-bang) grenades banned by RCW 10.116.040?
cards.a: No. The ban covers explosive/incendiary grenades designed to injure or kill. Non-explosive grenades that temporarily incapacitate or disorient (stun, sting, smoke, tear gas, blast ball) are excluded from the definition.

cards.q: What does "reasonably identifiable" mean in RCW 10.116.050?
cards.a: The uniform clearly displays the officer's name or other information the public can see and the agency can use to identify the officer.

cards.q: Four conditions to start a pursuit under RCW 10.116.060(1) (post-I-2113)?
cards.a: (a) Reasonable suspicion the person violated the law; (b) pursuit necessary to identify or apprehend; (c) the person poses a threat to others and the risk of not apprehending outweighs the pursuit risk; (d) immediate supervisor notification and oversight, considering alternatives and safety factors (speed, weather, traffic, roads, minors in the car).

cards.q: When may you shoot at a moving vehicle under RCW 10.116.060(4)?
cards.a: Only when necessary to protect against an imminent threat of serious physical harm from the operator's or a passenger's use of a deadly weapon. The vehicle is a deadly weapon only if the driver is using it as one and no other reasonable means to avoid the harm are immediately available.

cards.q: Can a WA judge issue a no-knock warrant?
cards.a: No. RCW 10.31.040(2) bars officers from seeking and courts from issuing any search or arrest warrant with an express exception to giving notice of office and purpose.

cards.q: Under RCW 10.31.040(1), when may an officer break a door to arrest?
cards.a: After giving notice of his or her office and purpose and being refused admittance.

cards.q: General rule for warrantless misdemeanor arrests in WA?
cards.a: Only when committed in the officer's presence, unless an RCW 10.31.100 exception applies (e.g., physical harm or threats, property taking, trespass, certain traffic crimes, DV order violations).

cards.q: When is a DV arrest mandatory under RCW 10.31.100(2)(d)?
cards.a: Suspect is 18+, within the preceding four hours assaulted a family or household member or intimate partner, and the officer believes a felonious assault occurred, an assault caused bodily injury (observable or not), or an act was intended to cause reasonable fear of imminent serious bodily injury or death.

cards.q: Name three diversion options under RCW 10.31.110.
cards.a: Crisis stabilization unit or 23-hour crisis relief center (12-hour hold, exam within 3 hours); referral to a designated crisis responder; release on agreement to voluntary outpatient treatment; referral to mobile crisis or the regional diversion/recovery navigator program.

cards.q: When does RCW 10.79.015(3) require a subpoena instead of a search warrant?
cards.a: When the evidence is held by a radio/TV station, newspaper, magazine or wire service (or their employees), unless there's probable cause the holder may be involved in the crime or the evidence would be destroyed or hidden.

cards.q: What is the penalty in RCW 10.79.040 for searching a home without a warrant?
cards.a: A gross misdemeanor for the officer.

cards.q: Define "deadly force" (RCW 9A.16.010).
cards.a: The intentional application of force through firearms or any other means reasonably likely to cause death or serious physical injury.

cards.q: Under RCW 9A.16.020(1), when is an officer's force not unlawful?
cards.a: When necessarily used by a public officer performing a legal duty (or a person assisting and acting under the officer's direction).

cards.q: What is the "good faith" standard in RCW 9A.16.040(4)?
cards.a: An objective standard: considering all facts known to the officer at the time, would a similarly situated reasonable officer have believed deadly force was necessary to prevent death or serious physical harm to the officer or another.

cards.q: Before deadly force to arrest under RCW 9A.16.040(1)(c), what must the officer have?
cards.a: Probable cause that the suspect, if not apprehended, poses a threat of serious physical harm to the officer or others (e.g., threatens with or displays a weapon, or committed a crime involving serious physical harm). Warn if feasible before using it to prevent escape.

cards.q: Two situations where homicide by a private person is justifiable (RCW 9A.16.050)?
cards.a: (1) Lawful defense of self or others present with reasonable ground to fear a felony or great personal injury and imminent danger; (2) actual resistance of an attempted felony on the slayer or in the dwelling where they are.

cards.q: Name the six circumstances in RCW 10.93.070 when you can enforce the law outside Federal Way.
cards.a: Written consent of the local chief/sheriff; emergency with an immediate threat to life or property; mutual-aid agreement or request from an officer with authority; transporting a prisoner; executing an arrest or search warrant; fresh pursuit.

cards.q: Does "fresh pursuit" (RCW 10.93.120) require immediate pursuit?
cards.a: No. It means pursuit without unreasonable delay.

cards.q: What does RCW 10.93.190 require when you see another officer use excessive force?
cards.a: Intervene when in a position to do so to end or prevent it, render aid to anyone injured at the earliest safe opportunity, and report the wrongdoing to a supervisor. Retaliation for good-faith intervention or reporting is prohibited.

cards.q: How does RCW 10.93.190 define "excessive force"?
cards.a: Force that exceeds the force permitted by law or by the policy of the witnessing officer's agency.

cards.q: Name three grounds for mandatory decertification under RCW 43.101.105(2).
cards.a: E.g., termination after unlawful force that caused death or serious injury; termination after failing to intervene in or report excessive force; termination for knowingly false statements (perjury, false reports, hiding evidence); disqualifying convictions; being prohibited from possessing weapons.

cards.q: Elements and level of Obstructing (RCW 9A.76.020)?
cards.a: Willfully hinders, delays or obstructs a law enforcement officer in the discharge of official powers or duties. Gross misdemeanor.

cards.q: Classification of Disarming a Law Enforcement Officer (RCW 9A.76.023)?
cards.a: Class C felony; class B felony if the firearm is discharged when removed.

cards.q: Resisting Arrest (RCW 9A.76.040): key element and level?
cards.a: Intentionally preventing or attempting to prevent a peace officer from lawfully arresting the person. Misdemeanor.

cards.q: What makes a statement "material" under RCW 9A.76.175?
cards.a: A written or oral statement reasonably likely to be relied upon by a public servant in the discharge of official powers or duties.

cards.q: Assaulting an on-duty officer in WA is what crime and class?
cards.a: Assault in the third degree, RCW 9A.36.031(1)(g) (if not 1st or 2nd degree). Class C felony.

cards.q: Elements of Attempting to Elude (RCW 46.61.024)?
cards.a: Driver willfully fails or refuses to stop immediately and drives recklessly while attempting to elude a pursuing police vehicle after a visual or audible signal to stop; the officer is in uniform and the vehicle has lights and siren. Class C felony.

cards.q: Standard for an officer-initiated emergency detention under RCW 71.05.153(2)?
cards.a: Reasonable cause to believe the person, because of a behavioral health disorder, presents an imminent likelihood of serious harm or is in imminent danger because of being gravely disabled. Deliver immediately to an approved facility; it may hold up to 12 hours.

cards.q: Is a stop pretextual if the officer also wanted to investigate a crime (Arreola)?
cards.a: Not if a reasonably suspected traffic infraction was an actual, conscious and independent cause of the stop. Pure pretext (Ladson) is still unlawful.

cards.q: What are the Ferrier warnings and when are they required?
cards.a: Before entering a home on a knock-and-talk to get consent to search: you may refuse consent, you may revoke it at any time, and you may limit the scope.

cards.q: Can you search a car incident to arrest in WA once the arrestee is cuffed in your patrol car?
cards.a: No (Valdez). The exception exists only for officer safety or preserving evidence the arrestee could reach; get a warrant or another exception.

cards.q: Does WA recognize Gant's 'evidence of the offense' branch for vehicle searches (Snapp)?
cards.a: No. Under article I, section 7 there is no such exception.

cards.q: What does Z.U.E. require before a Terry stop on a tip?
cards.a: Indicia of reliability (informant reliability or factual basis) or corroboration of more than innocuous facts suggesting criminal activity.

cards.q: How did Sum change the WA seizure test?
cards.a: The objective observer considers the person's race and ethnicity and knows bias contributes to disproportionate police contacts.

cards.q: Does WA recognize a good-faith exception to the exclusionary rule (Afana)?
cards.a: No.

cards.q: Was a short late-night visit to a suspected drug house enough for a stop (Doughty)?
cards.a: No. Without more specific facts it is not reasonable suspicion.

cards.q: What is Gunwall used for?
cards.a: Deciding whether the WA Constitution independently gives broader rights than the U.S. Constitution, using six nonexclusive factors.

cards.q: If officers shoot a driver who keeps going and escapes, was there a seizure (Torres)?
cards.a: Yes. Physical force applied with intent to restrain is a seizure even if the person escapes.

cards.q: Is hot pursuit of a misdemeanant always enough for warrantless home entry (Lange)?
cards.a: No. It's case-by-case; there must be an actual exigency.

cards.q: Is there a community-caretaking exception for entering homes (Caniglia)?
cards.a: No. Use emergency aid or exigent circumstances analysis instead.

cards.q: What are Gant's two branches, and which one does WA reject?
cards.a: (1) Unsecured arrestee within reach; (2) reasonable to believe evidence of the arrest offense is in the vehicle. WA rejects (2) (Snapp).

cards.q: Can you search an arrestee's phone data incident to arrest (Riley)?
cards.a: Generally no; get a warrant (case-specific exigency aside).

scenarios.title: Barricaded armed subject after a DV call
scenarios.setting: Night shift, Federal Way. You are first arriving to a residential apartment after a domestic-violence 911 hang-up. A neighbor says the male half, wanted on a local DV no-contact order, is inside with a handgun, yelling that he will not come out. No one else is believed to be inside. He is not answering the phone.
decision_points: Do you enter immediately?
How do you set the perimeter, CP, medical, and media?
What may you say if he starts talking?
When and how is V-SWAT requested?
If he puts the gun to his own head and never points it at officers or others, may you use deadly force?
scenarios.model_answer: Do not enter the space he controls unless it is necessary to protect lives other than his (MOS 46.1.10). Notify the field supervisor immediately. Build an inner perimeter (two-officer posts if staffing allows) and an outer perimeter for ingress/egress and bystanders. You are IC until the supervisor takes over. After the inner perimeter is up, attempt contact and ask him to surrender; promise only a safe detention if he complies — no other promises. Put the CP between the inner and outer perimeters, with room for specialty teams. Stage medical inside the outer / outside the inner, often near the CP. Keep media away from the CP and ask them not to air tactics. Notify the on-duty commander or CDO; the commander decides on Phase II/III and, if SWAT is necessary, contacts the designated Valley Commander to activate V-SWAT (46.1.10). CIS can start warrant/intel work; PIO as needed. Evacuate the outer-perimeter residences if reasonably possible and interview evacuees. This meets FWPD's operational barricade definition (definable space, armed, not complying with communication). Deadly force is not authorized against a person who is a danger only to himself (MOS 4.4.15, 4.4.18). Use time, distance, cover, Crisis Communications, and less-lethal options consistent with Chapter 4 and RCW 10.120. Activate your BWC (41.3.8). If this started as a DV, 41.2.8 still governs the underlying case once he is in custody.
scenarios.oral_board_hook: This is the most likely 'walk me through it' tactical question. Emphasize life priority, no freelance entry, no extra promises, and the SWAT/IC handoff.

scenarios.title: High-risk arrest warrant at a third-party residence
scenarios.setting: Detectives have a felony arrest warrant for a robbery suspect. A reliable source says he is staying at his girlfriend's apartment in a neighboring Valley city. The risk matrix (team SOP — not in these MOS chapters) comes back high: he is believed armed. V-SWAT is asked to serve it. You are a patrol officer assigned to assist, and you hope to be on the team.
decision_points: What warrant is legally required to enter her apartment?
What FWPD steps are required before you go (deconfliction, vest, BWC, host-city notification)?
May the warrant be written as no-knock?
What do you do at the door?
If you later find evidence in a room you should not have entered, can you save it with 'we would have found it anyway'?
scenarios.model_answer: This is a Steagald problem, not a Payton problem: an arrest warrant is not enough to enter a third party's home. You need a search warrant for her apartment, unless there is valid consent or a true exigency (Steagald, 451 U.S. 204 (1981); Payton, 445 U.S. 573 (1980)). You may not seek a no-knock warrant (RCW 10.31.040(2)). Before a nonconsensual entry, follow Coyle / RCW 10.31.040: announce identity, demand admittance, announce purpose, and be refused (expressly or by implication); learn Valley SWAT's trained wait time. Because the address is outside Federal Way and this is a preplanned tactical operation, MOS 46.2.9 requires command-level-to-command-level notification of the host agency before initiation. Coordinate IC, comms, media, follow-up, traffic, radio, and extra resources; the operating agency still approves tactics. Enter the operation into RISSafe as soon as the information is available and before you go (46.2.8; 800-952-5258). Plainclothes and uniformed personnel wear vests — warrant service makes a vest mandatory even for non-uniformed officers (41.3.5). Activate BWCs for the pre-planned warrant (41.3.8). If the search later exceeds the warrant, Washington does not recognize inevitable discovery (Winterstein, 167 Wn.2d 620 (2009)); get the warrant and the search right the first time.
scenarios.oral_board_hook: Shows you can combine constitutional law, the no-knock statute, and the practical MOS steps (vest, BWC, RISSafe, host-city command notification).

scenarios.title: Hostage in a small commercial shop
scenarios.setting: A robbery goes bad at a storefront. The suspect has a clerk at knifepoint, has locked the front door, and is yelling demands. Customers fled. You are the first officer.
decision_points: Is this a hostage situation under FWPD policy? Under RCW 10.116.030?
Do you immediately make entry to rescue the clerk?
What is the containment and notification sequence?
If commanders later consider CS gas, what legal steps apply?
scenarios.model_answer: Yes, this is a hostage situation under MOS 46.1.10 (held against her will by force or threat of force) and under RCW 10.116.030(4)(c) (held against her will by an armed or otherwise dangerous suspect). Do not make a freelance entry into the space he controls except as necessary to protect lives other than the suspect's, consistent with Chapter 4 (46.1.10). Contain (inner/outer perimeter), become IC until relieved, notify the supervisor and commander, request V-SWAT through the Valley Commander if the commander so decides, request CIS, PIO, medical staged inside the outer perimeter, and surrounding-agency notification via Valley Com. Attempt contact after the inner perimeter is up; promise only a safe detention if he complies. Peaceful resolution whenever reasonably possible. If tear gas is later considered, it is legally available only if necessary to alleviate a present risk of serious harm from this hostage situation, and only after the four RCW 10.116.030(2) steps (exhaust alternatives, supervisor authorization, announcement, time and space to comply). MOS 46.1.10's civil-disturbance gas language does not replace those statutory steps. Once SWAT arrives, SWAT takes the inner perimeter; the IC retains the incident (46.2.1).
scenarios.oral_board_hook: Tests whether you will 'go hero' versus contain, and whether you know the tear-gas statute is tighter than the civil-disturbance sentence in Ch. 46.

scenarios.title: Active assault at a high school
scenarios.setting: Daytime. Multiple 911 calls of gunfire in a Federal Way high school. You are 30 seconds out; a second officer is about a minute behind. Information is conflicting.
decision_points: Do you wait for a four-person team?
What is the first priority, and what do later arriving officers do?
What if you find the shooter down or contained and a locked classroom will not open?
What notifications and public-warning steps come next?
scenarios.model_answer: This is MOS 46.1.11. Commissioned personnel respond (Phase I). Keep lanes open for extraction. First priority: stop the killing. First arriving officers enter and move to the killer as contact team 1, even individually — you do not wait to build a full team while people are being actively killed. Don visible POLICE markings if you are in plain clothes. Arrest a compliant suspect; use force that overcomes resistance; isolate and contain a non-compliant suspect who is no longer actively killing, which may transition you into 46.1.10 barricade/hostage protocols; mark IEDs and leave them for BDU; report gunfire; watch for secondary attacks. After contact 1 is in, everyone else goes to staging for assignment. Establish IC, a staging manager, and staging; request mutual aid and Fire/medics there. Medical: treat in place with a cover officer, and/or CCP with dedicated protection, and/or rescue task force. A lieutenant arriving after contact 1 goes to the CP and becomes IC until a commander takes over. The commander or CDO can activate V-SWAT through the Valley Commander, call CIS and consider VIIT, and start public warning (PIO, social media, CodeRed, signage). For a school, designate a parent-student reunification center and send officers to hospitals for ID, security, and evidence. This is also where 4.4.1 n.14 fits: people with the least power to end the lethality (students) get the highest priority.
scenarios.oral_board_hook: The 'do you wait?' question. Policy says go to the killer first, then transition to barricade protocols if the killing has stopped.

scenarios.title: Mutual aid / V-SWAT warrant outside Federal Way
scenarios.setting: V-SWAT will serve a high-risk search warrant at a known address in another Valley city. You are on the entry team. A junior teammate says, 'It's our warrant, we don't need to tell them the plan.'
decision_points: Is notification required, and at what rank?
Who approves tactics?
What must be coordinated in advance?
Does this process apply to a fresh pursuit into that city?
scenarios.model_answer: The junior teammate is wrong about notification, and only half-right about tactics. MOS 46.2.9 requires that a FWPD command-level liaison (Commander / Acting Commander, Deputy Chief, or Chief) contact a command-level officer at the host agency (Commander, or Lieutenant or higher in agencies with sergeants as first-line supervisors) before initiating a preplanned tactical operation outside primary jurisdiction. The host agency is entitled to notification, input into operational decisions in their city, and a chance to share officer-safety information. The agency conducting the operation remains responsible for approving all tactics and operational decisions. Before going, coordinate at a minimum: named IC, communications representatives, media, follow-up investigation, traffic/crowd control, radio channel and monitor, and additional resources. Also deconflict in RISSafe (46.2.8). Fresh pursuit is excluded from the 46.2.9 'preplanned tactical operation' definition, so a running pursuit into the next city is not this process — but a planned warrant is.
scenarios.oral_board_hook: Regional-team maturity: you can be firm about tactics while still doing the courtesy and safety notification the MOS requires.

scenarios.title: Vehicle flight after a failed high-risk stop; shooting at the car
scenarios.setting: A felony suspect flees a pre-stop in a passenger car, weaving through late-evening traffic in Federal Way at high speed. A partner yells, 'Take the shot, Scott v. Harris lets us end this.' Another unit asks to box him in. Someone suggests the SWAT truck join as a fourth pursuit vehicle.
decision_points: May you pursue under FWPD policy? Under the current RCW?
May you fire at the car under Scott or Plumhoff?
May you box him in? PIT? Ram? Use the SWAT truck?
What must you radio, and who can kill the pursuit?
scenarios.model_answer: If you reasonably suspect or have PC for a felony (or DUI), FWPD 41.2.2 may authorize a pursuit, provided you meet the driver qualifications (EVOC within 24 months with risk-analysis training, certified in at least one intervention tactic, uniformed, authorized emergency-equipped vehicle), you immediately notify a supervisor who maintains oversight, you develop a plan to end the pursuit, and you continuously reassess. Current RCW 10.116.060 (I-2113) is broader than FWPD policy; still follow the stricter policy. Eluding alone would not be enough under 41.2.2.B. Scott and Plumhoff do not authorize the shot. You may not fire upon a moving vehicle unless necessary to protect against an imminent threat of serious physical harm from the operator's or a passenger's use of a deadly weapon; the vehicle itself is a deadly weapon only if used as one and no other reasonable means to avoid serious harm are immediately available (MOS 4.1.5, 4.4.18; RCW 10.116.060(3)). Move out of the path when feasible; do not shoot to disable the vehicle; each discharge must be justified. Boxing-in requires supervisor/commander approval and is off the table if you have reason to believe the person is armed with a firearm. PIT at or under 40 mph is available to trained officers; over 40 mph needs the monitoring supervisor's authorization. Ramming or a roadblock requires deadly-force-level circumstances and supervisor/commander approval. The SWAT truck may not pursue (41.2.2.E.4). Normally max three vehicles. Activate lights, siren, and BWC. Radio unit ID, that you are in a pursuit, the crime, location/speed/direction, and vehicle description. The primary officer, supervisor, or commander can terminate if the danger outweighs the need, the suspect is identified for later arrest, conditions make it futile, or you lose the vehicle.
scenarios.oral_board_hook: The answer that gets you hired is: 'I know the federal cases, and I still follow Washington law and FWPD policy, which are stricter.'

scenarios.title: Duty to intervene and first aid after a piled-on arrest
scenarios.setting: After a warrant subject is taken to the ground in a hallway, three officers are on top of him. He has stopped fighting. One officer is still kneeling on his back and starts to deliver knee strikes to the head 'to get the other hand out.' A spit guard is about to go on; he is gagging. Your CEW was discharged once and a probe is in his chest, not a sensitive area.
decision_points: What is your duty regarding the back pressure and the head strikes?
Spit guard and positioning?
CEW probe and medical care?
Reporting and UOF paperwork?
scenarios.model_answer: Intervene. MOS 4.4.9 / RCW 10.93.190: an identifiable on-duty officer who witnesses excessive force shall intervene when in a position to do so, and shall report wrongdoing to a supervisor. MOS 4.4.11: do not put prolonged pressure on the chest, neck, or back; roll him to the side and toward an upright position that does not impede breathing (unless unconscious); monitor breathing, color, and what he says; designate a Safety Officer if possible; do not transport prone. MOS 4.4.14: head strikes are not a pain-compliance tool — only self-defense or defense of others. MOS 4.4.19: do not apply a spit guard if he has labored or distressed breathing or is vomiting; if one is already on and he vomits or cannot breathe, remove it; seated or side recovery and monitor. Remove the non-sensitive CEW probe yourself with biohazard precautions, request EMS, and provide or facilitate first aid at the earliest safe opportunity (4.1.10, 4.4.10, 4.4.12). This is a reportable use of force (strikes, CEW discharge, possible complaint of injury). Tell the supervisor as soon as the scene is controlled, write a supplement, expect a UOF Review within 10 days, and a Significant Incident email before end of shift (4.1.11). If you used a hobble, do not hog-tie and do not leave him face-down (4.4.20).
scenarios.oral_board_hook: Integrity plus medical aftercare. Boards listen for whether you will stop a teammate.

scenarios.title: Clan lab / hazmat on a warrant
scenarios.setting: On a narcotics search warrant, you open a bedroom door and immediately smell chemicals, see glassware, and feel your eyes burn. A teammate starts to walk in 'just to make sure nobody is hiding.'
decision_points: Do you continue the search?
Who has command?
What notifications and perimeter steps follow?
scenarios.model_answer: Stop. MOS 46.1.10 clandestine-lab practice: withdraw quickly but safely, detain anyone already located, do not touch anything and do not attempt to alter the environment, immediately notify the field supervisor and the Fire Department, and establish an inner perimeter to prevent entry. Hazmat: Fire and their HazMat team have scene management and command authority; police stay back, evaluate from a safe distance, then support evacuation, traffic, and perimeter. A patrol supervisor responds to Fire's CP. Do not 'clear the room' through a working lab. If this address is outside the city, 46.2.9 host-agency coordination is already supposed to be in place; still get Fire and the supervisor now. First aid for exposure at the earliest safe opportunity (4.1.10).
scenarios.oral_board_hook: Discipline under uncertainty: get out, don't touch, notify, contain.

scenarios.title: Civil disturbance and proposed CS gas
scenarios.setting: A lawful demonstration downtown has turned into window-breaking and a crowd advancing on officers. A sergeant says, 'Get the CS out and push them.' You have a clear street behind the crowd. The mayor has not been contacted.
decision_points: May first arriving officers try to disperse the crowd now?
What must happen before dispersal tactics?
Is CS 'tear gas,' and what does the RCW require — especially for an outdoor riot?
scenarios.model_answer: First officers should not attempt dispersal without sufficient additional police assistance (46.1.10). Evaluate from a safe distance, notify Valley Com and a supervisor, and set a staging area. An order to disperse is to be given by the field supervisor before dispersal tactics. The commander takes IC and may use containment and dialogue, targeted arrests, or less-lethal force, but only with a clear path of escape, and gas/smoke/other less-lethal only by specially trained officers under coordinated control. CS is tear gas (RCW 10.116.030(4)(d); MOS 4.1.2(30)); OC is not. Tear gas may be used only if necessary to alleviate a present risk of serious harm from a riot, barricade, or hostage situation, and only after exhausting available appropriate alternatives, supervisor authorization, announcement, and time and space to comply. For a riot outside a jail, the highest elected official of the city — the mayor — must also authorize it (RCW 10.116.030(3)). MOS 46.1.10 does not mention the mayor or the four steps; the statute still controls. CDU may be the right regional resource (46.2).
scenarios.oral_board_hook: Statute over a thin policy sentence. Know that CS ≠ OC, and that an outdoor riot needs the mayor.

scenarios.title: Emergency-aid entry vs. a criminal investigation
scenarios.setting: Neighbors report yelling and a crash from an apartment. You hear no more noise. A detective on the radio says the resident is a burglary suspect they have been 'looking for a chance to talk to,' and tells you to 'go in on exigency and we'll sort it out. If we find the stolen property, inevitable discovery will cover it.'
decision_points: May you enter on emergency aid?
Does your subjective purpose matter in Washington?
Does inevitable discovery save a bad entry?
scenarios.model_answer: You may enter without a warrant only if the emergency-aid or other exigency tests are actually met — not because it is convenient. Federally, Brigham City is objective (serious injury or imminent serious injury). In Washington, Schultz and Boisselle require a genuine subjective belief that a present emergency needs immediate aid, that a reasonable person would believe the same, a nexus to the place, and no pretext for a criminal investigation. The detective's 'we've been looking for a chance' language is a red flag for pretext. If you do not have facts of a present emergency (sounds of ongoing violence, visible injury, a reliable report of someone hurt and untreated, etc.), stay out, try other contact, set a perimeter if needed, and get a warrant. Washington has no inevitable-discovery doctrine (Winterstein). If you later fire a shot, Mendez says an earlier unlawful entry does not automatically make the shot excessive force under the Fourth Amendment, but the entry is still its own problem, and Barnes plus RCW 10.120.010(8) still put your pre-force tactics into the totality. Do not create the emergency (King).
citations: County of Los Angeles v. Mendez, 581 U.S. 420 (2017)
scenarios.oral_board_hook: Shows you will not launder a search through a fake exigency, and that you know Washington is stricter than the Fourth Amendment.

oral.q: Why Valley SWAT, and why you, at this point in your career?
oral.framework: Structure: (1) service to the mission — resolving the worst calls with discipline so hostages, bystanders, and officers go home; (2) what you already do as a Federal Way patrol officer that transfers (first-arriving IC, scene organization, firearms and fitness work, night-shift decision-making); (3) specific preparation you have done (selection announcement, PAT and firearms standards, this policy study, dry-fire); (4) humility — you want to be a trainable operator, not a freelancer. Close by tying to MOS 46.2.1: the IC owns the incident, the SWAT Commander owns the team, and you want to be the person who makes that handoff cleaner, not noisier.
fill: [Your years at FWPD and prior relevant assignments or military/team experience]
[A specific patrol call where you slowed a scene down and organized it]
[Your current PAT / pull-up / firearms baseline and what you have improved since the announcement]

oral.q: Walk us through how you would articulate a use of force after a warrant entry or a barricade surrender that went hands-on.
oral.framework: Use a layered answer, in this order: lawful purpose (MOS 4.1.1 / RCW 10.120.020(1)); necessary — no reasonably effective alternative appeared to exist, and the force was reasonable and proportional (4.4.5); reasonable care and de-escalation that were possible, including one communicator and the 4.1.1(3)(b) characteristics; Graham factors (crime, threat, resistance/flight) from the viewpoint of a reasonable officer on the scene; the 4.1.6 force factors; termination when necessity ended; first aid at the earliest safe opportunity; paperwork (supplement, supervisor, Significant Incident, UOF review within 10 days). Mention that pointing a firearm is reportable (4.4.18; RCW 10.118.030) and that totality includes your own actions (4.1.2(31); Barnes).
fill: [A real arrest or force event you can discuss without gossip or pending-investigation problems]

oral.q: An armed barricaded subject has a gun to his own head and is not threatening anyone else. The team is asking for a green light. What is your analysis?
oral.framework: Start with the standard: deadly force only when necessary against an immediate threat of serious physical injury or death to the officer or another person — ability, opportunity, intent (4.1.1(2)). Then the bright-line policy: no deadly force against a person who is a danger only to themselves (4.4.15, 4.4.18); do not point or discharge a firearm at that person unless the triad toward the officer or another is present. Shift to what you would do: contain per 46.1.10, no freelance entry except to protect others, Crisis Communications, time/distance/cover, less-lethal if it meets Chapter 4 and will actually overcome the problem, medical staged. Do not invent a 'mercy' or 'stop the threat to himself' shot.
fill: [Any CIT or mental-health call you handled well — facts only]

oral.q: SWAT is on scene. A patrol lieutenant and the SWAT commander disagree about the next move. Who is in charge, and what do you do?
oral.framework: MOS 46.2.1 is clear: the SWAT Commander has full control of the deployment and use of SWAT members; the Incident Commander is responsible for the entire operation; the SWAT Commander reports to the IC at the CP and keeps the IC informed. You do not freelance, and you do not play the two against each other. If you have safety information (a squirter, a hostaged child, a radio problem), you push it to your team leader and to the CP. Inner-perimeter patrol should already be preparing to be replaced by SWAT as soon as practical.
fill: [A time you worked under unified or conflicting command and stayed in your lane while still passing critical information]

oral.topic: When to call SWAT / first-arriving actions
oral.q: You are first arriving. When do you know this is a SWAT call, and what do you do before the team gets there?
oral.framework: You do not 'activate SWAT' yourself. You recognize the 46.1.10 / 46.1.11 fact patterns (hostage; barricade — armed person in a definable space not complying; active assault), notify the supervisor, take IC, contain, and give the commander enough information to decide on Phase II/III and a Valley Commander activation. Before the team arrives: inner/outer perimeter, no entry except to protect others, no extra promises, CP between perimeters, medical staged correctly, evac and intel from neighbors, BWC on, keep radio discipline, start a crime/intel picture for CIS. For an active assault, first priority is stop the killing — that is the exception to 'wait for SWAT.'
fill: [A call where you were first arriving and set a perimeter or held a scene for specialists]

oral.q: Walk us through the legal steps for a high-risk warrant at a house that may not be the suspect's.
oral.framework: Whose house is it? Payton (arrest warrant + reason to believe the suspect is in his own home) vs. Steagald (search warrant for a third-party home). Confirm PC and particularity. You cannot seek a no-knock warrant (RCW 10.31.040(2)). At the door: Coyle steps — identity, demand admittance, purpose, refusal (express or implied) — and the team's trained wait time. Vest on, BWC on, RISSafe done, host-city 46.2.9 if outside Federal Way. No inevitable-discovery backup (Winterstein). If someone urges 'just go, Hudson says it won't get suppressed,' explain that Hudson is the federal exclusionary-rule case and does not control Washington statute or article I, section 7.
fill: [Any warrant you have served — your role, what you announced, what you learned]

oral.q: What do you do when a statute and a department policy do not say the same thing?
oral.framework: Follow the more restrictive rule that still complies with the law. Concrete examples from this study set: (1) Pursuits — I-2113 broadened RCW 10.116.060; FWPD 41.2.2 (rev. 12-08-2025) still limits you to felony or DUI and says eluding alone is not enough. You follow 41.2.2. (2) Tear gas — 46.1.10 is thin; RCW 10.116.030's four steps and the mayor's authorization for an outdoor riot still apply. (3) Barricade definitions — operational MOS definition vs. statutory tear-gas definition; use each for its purpose. (4) Deadly force — if Garner, 9A.16.040, and 10.120.020(2) conflict, MOS 4.1.3 says defer to 10.120.020(2). Never use a looser federal case (Scott, Plumhoff, Whren, Hudson) to talk yourself out of a Washington or FWPD limit.

oral.q: A teammate is using force that is no longer necessary, or is about to skip a required announcement. What do you do?
oral.framework: Stop it if you are in a position to do so, then report it. That is MOS 4.4.9 and RCW 10.93.190, not optional loyalty. Give a short example framework: verbal intervention first if it will work ('he's done, get off the back'), physical intervention if needed to prevent excessive force, medical care immediately, supervisor notification, truthful supplement. Boards are listening for whether you will risk short-term awkwardness to protect the subject, the teammate, and the team.
fill: [If you have ever intervened or reported — only what you can ethically discuss. If you have not, say so and still walk the policy.]

oral.q: The standard is hard. How are you preparing, and what happens if you have a bad day on the course or the PAT?
oral.framework: Be concrete and humble. Tie firearms to MOS 4.3 (annual proficiency is the floor, not the team standard; you only carry what you can qualify with) and to 46.2.2 (physical assessment and shooting qualification are required). Talk about your actual plan: dry-fire, live-fire on the VSWAT courses, PAT pacing, pull-ups, sleep around night shift. If you fail a course of fire, own the remedial-training mindset in 4.3.3 (you do not carry a weapon you cannot run; you train and re-test). Do not bluff standards that are not in the MOS (strict vs. kipping pull-ups, exact course times) — say what the announcement requires and what you have confirmed.
fill: [Your latest PAT numbers, pull-up max, and VSWAT pistol/carbine scores]

oral.q: When would you use a 40mm, a CEW, or gas, and what are the hard stops?
oral.framework: Lawful purpose + necessary + proportional + reasonable care, then tool-specific limits. 40mm/PIW: trained, biennial refresher, assess after each shot; do not intentionally aim at head, neck, chest, or groin, or engage an elevated subject without fall mitigation, unless deadly force is justified (4.4.17). CEW: support-hand, standard cycle ≤5 seconds, reassess, after three ineffective cycles consider something else; hard stops include flammables, moving-vehicle operators, elevated subjects, and (under 4.4.17) a restrained subject unless deadly force is authorized — note the tension with 4.1.9 and take the restrictive path. Gas: OC is not tear gas; CS/CN are. RCW 10.116.030 four steps, and the mayor for an outdoor riot. Head strikes and warning shots are not 'less-lethal ideas.'

oral.q: If a shooting happens, will the board or a court only look at the moment you pressed the trigger?
oral.framework: No. Barnes rejected moment-of-threat analysis; totality has no time limit. RCW 10.120.010(8) and MOS 4.1.2(31) include the officer's own actions leading up to the force. That is an argument for sound planning: approach, cover, announcements, less-lethal options staged, one communicator, no police-created exigency (King). Mendez means an earlier legal mistake does not automatically convert a later reasonable shot into 'excessive force,' but that earlier mistake is still its own problem and can still generate damages. You want neither problem.

oral.q: You have just been in an officer-involved shooting. What do you do in the next 30 minutes?
oral.framework: Safety and first aid first (4.1.10). Public safety statement only — enough to secure the scene and start the investigation — then limit discussion (4.1.11). Do not huddle-debrief with teammates. Weapons on the ground stay; you are not disarmed of a holstered weapon at the scene; expect a companion officer and later weapon collection with immediate sidearm replacement. Cooperate with the round count. Legal investigation is IIT/VIIT when death or substantial/great bodily harm results; you may consult an attorney before a detailed statement without unduly delaying it; peer support. Expect paid admin leave or reassignment (4.2.3), which is not a finding of fault. Activate/leave BWC per policy. Be truthful, brief, and medically useful.

oral.q: You work nights, then you will be on days. How will you show up trainable, and how do you handle a call that does not wait for the perfect plan?
oral.framework: Be honest about night-shift sleep, the January 1 shift change (Fri–Mon days), and how you have built study and training into those hours. Judgment: you will flex (MOS 41.2.1 lets you drop a priority response for safety or a stealth approach; 41.2.3 says you will not be disciplined for declining a PIT). You would rather be the operator who calls for a pause than the one who rushes a 46.1.10 entry. Give one short example of changing a plan because the facts changed.
fill: [A call where you changed the plan]

oral.q: What should we know about you that is not on the application, and is there anything you want to ask us?
oral.framework: Keep it specific and modest. One character story, one thing you are still working on, one intelligent question about the team (how inner-perimeter relief is practiced, how Crisis Communications is integrated, how the team trains announcement and wait time, how new operators are mentored). Do not ask only about gear or overtime. Do not pretend to have read team SOPs you have not been given.
hooks: gaps: team SOPs not in the MOS
fill: [A character example from patrol, training, or life that you are willing to have checked]

flags.item: MOS 46.2.2.B.3 and 46.2.4.B.1 end mid-sentence ('a review by the Chief of the pre-employment psychological'). The object of that review is not in the provided text.
flags.rec: Do not invent the missing words. Pull the complete pages from PowerDMS and Standards 21.3.2 (SWAT) and 16.2.2 (Crisis Communications / specialized assignment).

flags.item: SWAT selection refers to Standard 21.3.2; Crisis Communications refers to Standard 16.2.2. The earlier PowerDMS list mentioned 16.2.2 as selection for specialized assignment. These may be different standards. Neither was in the provided documents. 46.2.2 also does not contain PAT events, firearms course scoring, or the four selection phases from the announcement.
flags.rec: Pull both 16.2.2 and 21.3.2. Keep using the selection announcement for event standards and dates; do not pretend 46.2.2 is a complete selection SOP.

flags.item: Several stale internal cross-references: 46.1.10 cites 'Standard 1.3 Use of Force' (use of force is now Chapter 4); 4.2.1, 4.2.2, 4.2.3, and a 41.1.4 K-9 note still point to 'Standard 4.1.5' for post-force/reporting practices, but in the 05-18-2026 revision 4.1.5 is firing at vehicles and post-force practice is 4.1.11; 4.1.11's non-lethal reporting trigger cites 'Standard 4.1.4,' which is now the chokehold section (non-lethal is 4.1.9).
flags.rec: Follow the current section that actually contains the rule. Mention the stale cite only if a board reads from an older printout.

flags.item: No FWPD Standard 46.1.12 (jumps 46.1.11 to 46.1.13). No standalone FWPD text for CALEA 46.1.3–46.1.7 (only a compliance sentence in 46.1.2). No Standard 41.3.6 (jumps 41.3.5 to 41.3.7; 41.3.5 is annotated as CALEA 41.3.6).
flags.rec: Treat as numbering/CALEA mapping, not as a missing operational rule, unless PowerDMS shows withdrawn text.

flags.item: Still not in these documents: Valley SWAT interlocal agreement and team SOPs (activation criteria beyond 'the commander determines,' less-lethal and chemical-munitions SOP, NFDD/flash-bang SOP, TEMS integration, HNT coordination beyond 46.2.4, announcement/wait-time standard, risk-assessment matrix for high-risk warrants). 46.2.3 assigns specialized equipment to SWAT and requires quarterly inspection but does not inventory it.
flags.rec: Those remain a PowerDMS / team-manual pull, as in the original earlier list. Do not invent munitions rules.

flags.item: Frequently referenced but not provided: MOS 12.1.2 (command notification), 16.2.2, 21.3.2, 22.2.4 (line-of-duty death or serious injury), Chapter 26 (discipline/UOF routing), Chapter 52 (investigations), 81.2.5 (Code 2 / Code 3 definitions), 61.3.3 (escorts), 41.2.4 detail, Guild contract articles, VIIT Organization and Operational Manual, training bulletin 17-002, Authorized Equipment and Apparel Table, Special Purpose Vehicle table, Respiratory Protection Program, Greater Federal Way Community EOC Plan.
flags.rec: Pull 12.1.2, 16.2.2, 21.3.2, and the VIIT manual first after selection paperwork; they come up in almost every critical-incident standard.

flags.item: RCW 10.116.060, as amended by Initiative 2113 (2024 c 6), allows a pursuit on reasonable suspicion of a law violation plus necessity and a risk-balance test (and supervisor/training conditions). FWPD 41.2.2, revised 12-08-2025 — after I-2113 — still authorizes pursuits only for a felony or DUI and says eluding alone is not enough.
flags.rec: This is probably intentional agency tightness, not an error, but it is a real difference. Follow 41.2.2. If a board asks about 'the law,' distinguish the statute from the policy. Confirm with a supervisor or training unit that 41.2.2 is the current enforced rule.

flags.item: FWPD 46.1.10's operational barricade definition requires a weapon (or direct access to a deadly weapon) and non-compliance with communication. RCW 10.116.030(4)(a)'s tear-gas definition of 'barricaded subject' does not require that the person be armed. Hostage definitions also differ slightly (MOS: force or threat of force; statute: armed, potentially armed, or otherwise dangerous suspect).
flags.rec: Use each definition for its purpose. Confirm how Valley SWAT trains the distinction. Do not use the MOS armed-requirement to skip the statutory tear-gas analysis, or the statutory unarmed barricade definition to automatically launch a 46.1.10 armed-barricade response.

flags.item: MOS 46.1.10's civil-disturbance section allows coordinated, trained use of 'gas, smoke, or other less lethal devices' with a clear escape path, but does not reprint RCW 10.116.030's four steps or the mayor's authorization for an outdoor riot. Chapter 4 defines tear gas and excludes OC, but does not set out the deployment steps.
flags.rec: Always apply RCW 10.116.030 in addition to 46.1.10. Pull any FWPD or V-SWAT chemical-munitions SOP when available.

flags.item: MOS 4.4.17 says an ECW should not be used on a handcuffed or otherwise restrained person unless deadly force is authorized. MOS 4.1.9 allows a contact CEW application on a handcuffed subject who remains combative, and allows a cartridge discharge only if a person handcuffed behind the back is attempting escape and escape would create an imminent public threat.
flags.rec: Flag the tension. Default to the more restrictive reading until current defensive-tactics training resolves it: no cartridge deployment on a restrained person unless the 4.1.9 escape/imminent-threat facts, or deadly force, are present.

flags.item: MOS 4.4.6 lists 'execute any other community caretaking function' as a lawful purpose for physical force. MOS 4.1.1 / RCW 10.120.020(1) do not list caretaking as an enumerated physical-force purpose; 4.1.1(5) / 10.120.020(5) say the statute does not limit lifesaving or community-caretaking functions.
flags.rec: Do not treat caretaking as a blank check for force. Stay inside the 4.1.1(1) purposes plus genuine lifesaving measures.

flags.item: MOS 4.1.9 says PIWs are used 'in adherence to the restrictions listed below,' but in the extract the immediately following lines only cover accessibility and a missing-weapon notification. Detailed PIW restrictions appear in 4.4.17.
flags.rec: Use 4.4.17 as the restriction set. If a cleaner PDF page exists in PowerDMS, check for a dropped bullet list in 4.1.9.

flags.item: Earlier earlier study notes referred to a 30-second duty-to-intervene timing figure. MOS 4.4.9 in this revision does not include a 30-second rule.
flags.rec: Do not recite a 30-second rule from this chapter. If another directive or lesson plan still uses that figure, cite that source, not 4.4.9.

flags.item: How Kentucky v. King applies under article I, section 7 was already flagged in earlier as something to confirm with a DPA or legal advisor. This study set does not invent a Washington holding that was not briefed.
flags.rec: Know the federal rule and the fact that WA privacy law is often stricter. Confirm before relying on King in an affidavit or an interview.

flags.item: VSWAT firearms course scoring zones, strict vs. kipping pull-ups, and burpee standards are still not in these policy documents (same gap as Week 1).
flags.rec: Use the qualification course sheets and the selection announcement, not the MOS, for those numbers.
